utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and I greet all of the people in the courtroom, Mr. Scott, all of the Defence counsels, the accused, and everyone else in this room, as well as those who are not in the courtroom. We shall pursue now our work, pursue the cross-examination; but before we do, I know that Mr. Murphy and Mr. Karnavas would like to take the floor on a number of topics. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the court. I left yesterday the courtroom rather depressed, to say the least, and the reason for that was I was rather disappointed in being overly energetic in responding to Judge Trechsel's shaking of his head and trying cutting me off while I was trying to make my argument in response to the Prosecution's objection. I was upset at my own behaviour because it through me off, but it is something that occurs over and over again, and justice has to be seen to be done, not just to be done. Over the past 17 months, there have been instances where it would appear, at least to those watching this trial and to the accused that at least one member of the Trial Bench seems to be rather energetic in expressing his feelings and yesterday was one example. I was in the process of responding to an objection. The objection was a rightful objection. The Prosecution was exercising his rights, and it dealt with the issue of relevance. The issue of relevance, of course, was raised by myself and others in our objection, and I raised it again at the commencement of the proceedings yesterday morning. The Trial Chamber -- that if we went into a certain area, we would be opening up a Pandora's box. And after 17 months of testimony, the Judges should know what is and is not relevant before even hearing the testimony; and then, as far as weight goes, they can determine that at the end of the trial. Be that as it may, I felt that I was in my proper rights in defending Dr. Prlic to respond to the objection. I sat there. I listened to Mr. Scott. He was able to say what he had to say. There were no gesticulations from the Bench. He was allowed to say his piece, and then I proceeded and, of course, I was cut off. And one of the reasons was, was point out by Judge Trechsel, that the gentleman was a historian and not a lawyer and I was asking for legal questions. So, I went back home and I thought about this a little bit, because yesterday, in the heat of the moment, I wasn't thinking as quickly as I should have been. But I should have point out, Where was Judge Trechsel, for instance, when we had Mr. Tomljanovich, another historian from Yale? Where was he to stop Mr. Tomljanovich from giving opinions on the law. Where was he to say something to Mr. Tomljanovich about going into areas of political science and other areas, which clearly he wasn't qualified? Tomljanovich was allowed to go into areas which were outside of history. He talked about the law repeatedly. He commented about the structures of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And, of course, the Trial Chamber in that instance allowed the Defence to challenge the gentleman on his credentials and to challenge them vigorously, which is the right thing to do. So, in other words, you can either cut him off at the pass and say you will not go into those areas or give the Defence an opportunity to respond. In that instance, I saw no response from the Bench. I mention this because, if you're sitting on this aisle of the court, the perception is when it's a Prosecution witness, there is no reaction; but if the Defence begins, as I did yesterday, in challenging the gentleman's knowledge about matters which he had commented and had reached opinions on, given his report, then, in the middle of my making a record without being heard and I'm trying to respond to an objection, going to relevancy, at that point, there is a prejudgement, and I think it's unfair. Now, as I've noted in the past, we've had other incidents. Yesterday, for instance, when Mr. -- just to give a couple of examples. Yesterday, when the issue came up that was raised by Mr. Kovacic with regard to the archives, we had the Prosecutor stand up. He made a reference to the Library of Congress, and it seemed at the same time Judge Trechsel had the Library of Congress in mind as well. Fair enough. You could see Judge Trechsel mouthing "library of Congress" before Mr. Scott mentioned it. It was harmless, but what is the perception? Two or three weeks ago, there was a witness and the question was posed: What did the prisoners have to eat? The mike was on in a rather cynical tone, and I underline that, there was a comment by Judge Trechsel, if anything. My client picked it up. I said nothing. I looked at Judge Trechsel. I didn't say anything at the time, but my client brought it my attention and said, "Aren't you going to react." My comment was, "How can I possibly react? What can I possibly say?" And then he said, "Well, how am I getting a fair trial if these are the sort of comments made from the Bench." It may be a perfectly natural reaction under the circumstances or with the knowledge we have of the case; but if we're talking about the perception of justice, you know, then I think we all need to be a little bit more mindful and a little more careful. Whether justice will be done at the end of the trial, that's somebody else's -- we'll see. I don't know. Now, we do have options on the Defence side, as does the Prosecution. We also know that the Bench is awfully divided and has been divided for quite some time. Virtually all decisions, major decisions, seem to be split decisions, and we all know which way they go and who's voting on them. It's rather apparent. But I am concerned. I'm trying to do my job. I'm trying to do it properly. I don't like having to raise my voice against the Judge, but I don't think it is fair. I don't know it is proper for the Judge to sit there and basically bob their head, when it's the Prosecution talking; but when it's the Defence, gesticulating, saying no, because that's the appearance. And it gives the appearance to the accused that perhaps some members of the Bench are less open-minded than should be. I'm not suggesting that is the case. I don't know, but I am rather concerned. I'm very concerned; and perhaps, when we cool down a little bit, it may be good to have another session, maybe have a 65 ter hearing in private, but something has to be cleared up. I don't think it is appropriate for members of the Bench to be making comments while the mike is on and others can hear them, where they're voicing opinions. I don't think it's proper to be cutting off the Defence in the middle of responding to an objection, especially when there seems to be a double standard. You could certainly cut off Tomljanovich, but you chose not to do. None of the Bench did. You allow allowed him. You gave him free rein. When it comes to this gentleman, all of a sudden we need to be protective of him, because if the Prosecution says, "All we need is a date. It fits our little theory," therefore, okay, fine. It's all relevant. We already know about it. It seems to me that it's a rather cynical approach to take to say, "We don't know whether it's relevant or not. We're going to hear it." But when the Defence tries to demonstrate through proper cross-examination why it is not relevant, to cut the Defence off, so there is no record. That is my point. That is why I think that what happened yesterday was unfair. And I know that I'm taking a risk by bringing this to the Trial Chamber's attention, but my client is looking at me and is asking me, "What is going on." And I have to explain to him every day not to worry, that this Trial Bench is going to look at all the facts objectively. And while there may be some facial expressions or there may be some slips of the tongue, at the end of the day, they're going to be fair. But I must insist that we need, all of us, to be very mindful that justice has to be seen, not just done. And that's -- I bring it to the Court's attention, and I invite the Court to set a date so we can have a mini hearing on this issue, but I think it would be good to clear the air. That's all I have for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A few brief comments on what you have just said. A witness has testified upon the request of the Prosecution in order to answer questions relating to the facts or the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia during the period covered by the indictment, as well as following the period covered by the indictment. And yesterday, at some point, a legal question was raised, and my colleague, who, of course, will also take the floor if he wishes to, mentioned the fact that the witness is not a jurist, a legal expert, and it was, therefore, difficult for him to address legal questions since he is not trained to do so. That is what was said on that topic. I was not of the same opinion. I feel that a historian should generally have some legal knowledge. Nonetheless, I recognise that the transitional provisions of the Washington Agreement are so complex that it is not surprising that the witness was not aware of them. So that was the debate that took place yesterday on the topic of history and law. The second issue raised, well, it would seem that some time ago the context of Dretelj, the issue of the food given to the prisoners was raised, the issue of what the prisoners ate, and an element was mentioned that had already been mentioned in the context of other depositions. As far as I remember, some had indicated that the food was the same for the soldiers and the detainees. So what was said really didn't have any impact, any consequences. Now, as to the way in which justice is perceived, we all realise that the relevance and the probative value really have nothing to do with that. The ruling will be handed down based on the documents, the evidence, and the answers given to the questions, in light of the evidence submitted by the Defence when the time comes. So no one today is in a position to say that such and such a Judge feels a certain way on a certain issue. Things keep changing, and what seems like truth today may not be truth tomorrow. Elements -- new elements can change things, so we should not draw any conclusions at this point. The accused will be judged in the long run at the end, based on all of the elements that we have before us. For the time being, there are elements that are being discussed, and the final conclusion and ruling will only be adopted at the very end. So anyone who might feel that decisions have already been taken or are being taken, that minds are being made up, would be very much in the wrong. And that's all that I have to say about the issues that have been raised. I don't know whether my colleague would like to take the floor. I will give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will not try to address all the points counsel has saw fit to raise, but address two issues. One is the shaking of my head. Mr. Karnavas, I am not a poker player and I have not been born with a poker face, and I seem not to have really learned it. I remember at one point Ms. Nozica, and perhaps also Ms. Alaburic, certainly one of them stated that they liked to see an echo on my face of what they were bringing forward because it let them know where they were. I am not reacting consciously. I will try withhold any mimic reaction to what I'm thinking. But for one, when I was shaking my head, I was not stopping you, Mr. Karnavas, and that was not my intention at that point of stopping you. And if I disagree with something that you say, that doesn't mean that I am prejudiced on the issue of this trial alone. It is not reduced to what you say, Mr. Karnavas. On the other hand, as far as the position of the witness is concerned, what my objection still is - and we'll perhaps come back to that - it's not so much that the witness is trained as a historian rather than as a lawyer. It is a fact that the task assigned on the witness was a merely anthological task. That means he was asked to state what a historian today observes on the period after the Washington Agreement, and he was not asked to pass any value judgement on whether that was something that was wrong or unlawful or whatever. Now, the word "unlawful" does appear at one point, and I will have already leave of the President at the beginning of his continued interrogation to invite him to make clear what he means and where he gets that from. As you have noted, I was surprised. I haven't given it the weight as you have given it, which of course is your right, but I think there might have been a misunderstanding. I think that's all to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if I may briefly respond as far as the value judgement. If you look at the second report, which was the thrust of my cross-examination, it's full of value judgements. That's the problem. That's number one. And, number two, I understand what the task was; however, you cannot look at historical events in the abstract and in a vacuum. You have to put them in perspective. In my opinion, what the Prosecution is attempting to do is have the Trial Chamber draw certain conclusions. Now, they're entitled to have the Trial Chamber draw those conclusions, but what we're suggesting is: Please don't draw those conclusions until you hear all of the evidence in -- and all the historical facts perspective. And they can't bring in a witness and say: Well, this was my very limited task and don't go outside if, for instance, in trying to accomplish that task, one would be expected to look at other matters and to be aware of other facts. That was the whole point that I was trying to make yesterday, and that's why I believe we disagree on how far cross-examination should be. I don't believe that this is relevant testimony. You believe it is or maybe that it is. And the only way we're going to find out is the Prosecution is entitled to ask their questions. I didn't interrupt during their direct, but I'm entitled to go and then bring out other matters and, because, as I indicated, I'm being forced now to go into 1996, 1997, 1998, all the way to 2007 with respect to this, because the Prosecution yesterday, if I understood him correctly, their theory now is that the joint criminal enterprise that they believe existed continued to exist all the way at least until 1999, 2000, and maybe even today. That's their theory, which means I have to defend against that. If I don't have to defend against it, then there's no need to hear any testimony after the cut-off date of the indictment. It's plain and simple to me as a lawyer; but if we're going to go into that period and if that's going to be the argument, because I think the Prosecution's argument is grounded in that it was so embedded, this joint criminal enterprise was so embedded, that these -- these Croats just could not get along and can't get along and they're just persisting, well, if that's the case, fine, they can argue that. And I'm saying: Look at other historical facts. And if you're going to be looking at the Washington Agreement or if you're going to be looking at the Dayton Agreement, do so in context. What did they call for? What happened afterwards? What was going on in country? What was possible at the time? What were the internationals doing and still doing? Just think. I just invite the Trial Chamber to think back of the reunification of Germany, just as an example. In peacetime where Germany at that time was a powerhouse, their economy was the best in Europe, and think about all the problems it had. That's what we're talking about in a middle of a war in forming the Federation, and we're talking something like that multiplied by a hundred times after the war with respect to Dayton. So that's what I'm trying to do. I'm trying to give you the facts through cross-examination, because at the end I'm going to be arguing, at the end of this gentleman's testimony, that you should disregard everything; otherwise, we will turn this trial into a seminar on post-construction Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague would like to take the floor and then Mr. Scott will have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I have to speak up as well because the issues which had been taken up by Mr. Karnavas are very important ones, and we have to think about them and we have to give our own answer and really to take into account whatever he said. I, as for one, I am very much always watching Mr. Karnavas in a way with an approach that is very positive as far as his work is concerned. I am fully aware of his talented way of representing his client. I am fully aware of his knowledge; and also, as far as we know he's, president of the body of the council of the Defence. Now, I believe that that is why he has always a particular way of responsibility and important task to represent his client and to speak in this Chamber according to his achievements. By the way, I also used to read his articles and whatever he has written about the Defence issues in the Tribunal. On the other hand, I have also some problem that he is having a kind of leitmotif, a major push, a major line, according to which he always tries to prove that this trial is not fair, and I cannot accept this leitmotif. I cannot accept this approach. I really believe that we have to come to terms and have to understand each other, but, of course, we all know the important issues which are at hand. We all know that it is the basic task of the Bench to be independent, to be neutral, to listen to both the Prosecution and to the Defence, and to be really as objective as possible, as humanly as possible, by studying the issues at hand and then to make it's, I mean the Bench's, proper conclusions and decision. At the same time, I really believe that it will be not fair to characterize the work of the Chamber as not being fair in its approach towards the Defence, towards the client, their clients, to the accused, et cetera. And that is why I would like to speak up and to say that I continue to be on the side of the Bench which really would like to have a fair trial. It is our intention to do that and, therefore, we are asking the Defence, and especially I would like to ask Mr. Karnavas, not to be carried away by their own convictions, not to be carried away by their own oratory sometimes, but really to see that this Bench is constructed in a way which really give rise to the best hope of this Trial Chamber to achieve a judgement which is fair and fairly based. It is what I would like to say and I would not like to go into the details as far as the present witness's qualifications or what he has written and what he -- what he knows. I know something also about Dayton and Washington Agreement because, during that time in the 1990s, I was working in the Hungarian Foreign Ministry on the legal issues of the Balkan crisis and Bosnia-Herzegovina; therefore, I may claim that I know something about it. At the same time, I do not say and I do not claim that I know everything, and that is why I am, in the future as well, would like to study everything which is at our hands which is before us. I can pledge my full, I would say, attempt, not only attempt, but my approach, which is to be that we have to reach the conclusions which are fair and just. It is what I would like to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to all of you, and good morning to all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honours, I want to make a few, hopefully, brief comments in response to some things that have been said this morning, and I want it to be measured because I start off by saying, of course, the Defence has the right to make a record about concerns that they may have about the conduct of the trial and the rights of the accused. I understand that and that certainly has, of course, its legitimate place in the courtroom, and I start my comments with that. I also want to start my comments by saying I'm torn whether not to say anything at all because part of my instinct is not to belabour this and let's just get on with business. However, the problem is, Your Honour, as Mr. Karnavas has so often said, the parties have to make their record; and for better, for worse, some years from now, some Appeals Chamber or somebody else may be reading this record and it is important that the record be balanced. And if the Prosecution does not at least occasionally state its position, then we have a record in which it's only a statement of the Defence grievances over and over and over again, and not one that, in our judgement, reflects a fair state of the record as a whole. While I recognise the right of the Defence, including Mr. Karnavas, to state his positions, I think the way that it has been done repeatedly and they way it was done yesterday and again even this morning, albeit, albeit in a softer tone, the substance was no different. My concern is that this -- these theatrics, these positions are for the purpose of intimidating the Court, threatening the Court, having a chilling effect on the Court and the way it conducts its business. It's further to push the Chamber. It would be perceived by some outside the courtroom, and I guess what you see in the courtroom depends on where you sit, both inside the courtroom and outside. And I won't belabour that further, except to say that what Mr. Karnavas has said is his particular perspective and not necessarily the perspective of all the observers of these proceedings. It is unfair to push the Chamber into, with the greatest respect for Judge Prandler, to make him feel the need to on the one hand, of course, express his concerns about some of Mr. Karnavas's conduct, but at the same time, of course, appraise him: He's a very good lawyer, he's the president of the ADC, et cetera, et cetera. It shouldn't be necessary to say that, and I'm confident, but, on the other hand, I'm confident that Judge Prandler has the same high regard for the lawyers on the Prosecution team opinion. The fact that, by his comments, Mr. Karnavas would press the Chamber and press Judge Prandler, by one example, to feel the need to then praise Mr. Karnavas in a conduct -- in a situation which I do not believe deserved praise is unfair, unfair to the Prosecution, unfair to the proceedings as a whole. I also think it's terribly presumptuous, terribly presumptuous, for counsel to comment on the internal workings of the Chamber and whether there's a split among the Judges or whether there's a differences and to comment on that. Now, unless Mr. Karnavas has some inside track or inside source on how the Chamber conducts its business, I think that's inappropriate and entirely presumptuous to make those comments, and they shouldn't be made. Now, turning to what happened with the witness, as I said yesterday, Your Honour, the witness was tasked by the Prosecution to answer a particular question, as Judge Trechsel has pointed out. Now, If Mr. Karnavas has problems with that, which he may, he can direct that to me, he can direct that to the Prosecution, he can direct that to the Prosecution, and attack me and attack the work that was done. But it's not fair, in my view, in my respectful submission, to attack the witness, when the witness did what he was asked to do, a point that both the witness and I both repeatedly attempted to make yesterday. The issue, the only issue that the witness, once again, to belabour it one more time, was to research the existence -- the continuing existence and operation of Herceg-Bosna. Good or bad, right or wrong, justified or not, did it continue to exist and operate after Dayton and Washington? I think the answer is clearly: Yes, it did. It doesn't even appear to be disputed anymore. Maybe it was disputed at one pint, but now we're not disputing that but the answer is to try to justify it. That is the moving target that I talked about yesterday. I think it was -- I think the witness was treated unfairly yesterday. I hope he won't be treated unfairly today, and, Your Honour, I end my comments there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I had not, in fact, intended to speak now. It was a misunderstanding. I had asked for some time at the end of the day rather than at the beginning, but I think it may perhaps be in everyone's interest for someone to intervene who's not involved in the immediate heat of what happened yesterday. And I -- let me just say this on the issue of the witness. The Prosecution says: "Well, it's not proper to cross-examine this witness outside the bounds of what the limited task he was asked to do." But, Your Honour, I -- I don't think it's any secret that the Prosecution's intention in having this witness testify is going to be, at the end of the day, to suggest to the Trial Chamber that what was going on after Dayton was, in some sense, illegal and a continuation of the joint criminal enterprise. If that was not the intention, why have we taken two days to have this testimony at all? It would be completely irrelevant. And if that's the case, then for the Prosecution to say: "Well, you can't cross-examine the witness to see what the transitional arrangements were under Washington or under Dayton" is completely misconceived, because if you're going to ask: "Did Herceg-Bosna continue and what was it doing after a certain point," it has to be relevant to say: "Well, was there any role that it was foreseen Herceg-Bosna was going to fulfil?" I mean, what was the -- why was it continuing? What was its role, if any, in the post-Dayton world? And for a witness to come and represent himself to be an expert on the Balkan -- on Balkan history and the Balkan history of the former Yugoslavia and to say: "Well, I don't know these things. I didn't bother reading the Dayton Accord. I can't remember what it says," Your Honour, it's a matter which affects the weight of his testimony. And that will be a matter that the Trial Chamber will consider, one way or the other. But for Mr. Scott to say that "Well, you can't get into that and expose this weakness in the evidence," in my respectful submission, is completely misplaced. And I will respectfully submit that Mr. Karnavas was completely entitled to cross-examine. And, Your Honour, I don't think it would be constructive for me to comment on any broader issues, so I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Murphy. We are going to have the witness brought in. Mr. Usher, please bring him in. So I think that Mr. Karnavas still has another 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas, because I believe that Judge Trechsel had a follow-up question. Good morning, sir. Can you hear the -- me as I'm being translated? Judge Trechsel has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Miller, you have stated, I believe yesterday, that your report was an objective description of developments, yet Mr. Karnavas has pointed out that you speak of illegal structures in your second report. Can you explain to the Chamber how that gets into your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I also explained, my report is based on research accomplished by other organizations. The term "illegal" was drawn from the ICG report on reunifying Mostar. I -- one of the jobs of a scholar is to evaluate the evidence, to evaluate the materials he is using in preparing such a report. In that ICG report on reunifying Mostar, the argument is convincingly made that the authorities in Mostar, the Croatian authority, had systematically avoided implementation of agreements that they had entered into with the other parties in Bosnia under international guidance, and, therefore, the word "illegal" seemed to me to be applicable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Does that not cast a slightly different light on your report, in that you seem to endorse this finding by the institute and make a description which is not a mere description but which is tainted by such a value judgement? You not just observe whether Herceg-Bosna continues to exist, but without perhaps so saying so very expressly, but betraying your attitude, you at the same time say that it unlawfully continues to exist. Is that the correct interpretation of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't actually think that it betrays my bias, and I don't think that it betrays the bias of the ICG report that I'm relying on. I think that it shows -- I think that the ICG demonstrated that the Croatian authorities in Herceg-Bosna had avoided implementation of agreements. You know, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Miller, I am not talking of bias. One can be neutral and pass a value judgement. That does not exclude each other. But the issue is whether one makes a pure neutral description such as a camera would, and even there it's, of course, a bit doubtful whether it is entirely neutral, or whether in describing a situation one also says something about its value, more particularly, its lawfulness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually don't personally view a comment on lawfulness or legality a value judgement. A value judgement would be if I were to say, for instance, "Those lousy Croats in Mostar persisted in illegal behaviour." To me, that's a value judgement and I don't believe I entered into that sort of language in this report. However, I guess perhaps I would just say I disagree with your characterization, but I respect your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I think we have a semantic problem to some extent here, because we may have a cooler -- a cooler conception of value judgement. But thank you. That is -- that answers my question. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, but I don't think you have anything to object to this way of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, that was wonderful, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It shows you that you are -- you have a tendency to prematurely misjudge our minds, and I would invite you to be careful and take the lesson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I will take my own medicine. I want to thank Judge Prandler for his comments. I don't agree entirely with the Prosecution, but I am very mindful of our task at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Picking up on what Judge Trechsel indicated, first, let's begin with a definition. What do you define as value judgement? Because I have a couple of questions on this. Give me a definition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess I understand a value judgement to be a judgement -- I mean, it's almost self-evident, isn't it. A value judgement would be a judgement based on my own values of another person's or institution's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then picking up again from what was said in your response to Judge Trechsel's question, you said that you read certain reports, the research of a scholar. You sort of underscored that, the scholar part. That. The research you did is you went on the internet and pulled up some reports and you read them, right? That's the extent of your research? It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes we questions aren't yes or no. I mean, I suppose technically, yes, that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So technically that's what you did. And I take it when you were surfing the net technically what you did is you discriminated - I'm using that word in a nonperjorative fashion - but you discriminated as what you would download, look at, read, analyse, versus what you would not download, look, research, read, analyse, and synthesise into your report. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, we always discriminate based on our own knowledge of the sources and our understanding of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be one form of a value judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that an inflection at the end of my statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. Anyway. I'll move on. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't think that's actually a value judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you said that you looked at those reports; and based on their evidence, does that mean that you read their footnotes, or does that mean that you actually went beyond the footnotes and actually looked at the sources that these organizations used in citing and in basing their own conclusions? That's an easy one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noted the sources they used. I did not go back and re-read the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you read the footnotes and said: "Well, I guess if they're citing this newspaper, it must be correct; or if they're citing this report, it must be correct." There was no need for you to actually look at any original sources, as a scholar, but, rather, you read the report, you glanced at the footnote, and it was: "Okay. I think this report has value and I'm going to incorporate it into my little report." Basically, that's how it went, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not only how it went; that's what scholars do all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We accept -- for instance, you were showing Steven Burg and Paul Shoup's book the other day. We accept people based on their work. We accept their current work based on the reputation of their previous work. We do that because it's impossible to go back and actually examine every source that's been used over the decades in the case of historians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The process is one in which we all build on each other's work. People's work is judged by other people other scholars over time in the form of reviews, articles, critiques. So we develop an opinion. We develop a position on the value of a particular scholarly and other work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, yesterday - I don't want to belabour the point - but yesterday you did indicate that -- when I pushed you a little bit, you said, "I did what I was asked to do." This is on page 116, line 11: "I did what I was asked to do which is provide a short, direct report on the nature or persistence," or the nonpersistence I suppose, "of the government of Herceg-Bosna, and I did so as I was asked on the basis of open-source materials, knowing that I was not going to be able to afford or to be supported in going -- in going on-site research and ..." And so my question is at this point in time: Are you saying, in your answer here, that the Prosecution declined requests on your part to actually look at original source material or to go on site and maybe perhaps meet with some of the players in situ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not make a request. That's my assumption that it would not have been supported because the question itself was very basic and straightforward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you, being the historian, the expert, being asked to provide an answer to these questions, did you not think perhaps it is necessary for you to tell the client, that is, the Office of the Prosecution, what you, the expert, might want to look at, might need to look at in order to give a full, fair, complete, unbiased opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- excuse me, because the differences between writing a report that essentially states the obvious, that obvious has not really been contested here, or doing years and years of work --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- as a scholar --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that would result in something like a book-length manuscript, which I didn't as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- Before we get to your report, because we are going to pick up on that, I just want to finish up a little bit on what we were talking about yesterday, and that is the transitional process. My first question is: Would transfer of responsibilities to the New Federation Institution parallel -- was there a parallel process from Herceg-Bosna in institutions of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with the constitution of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you don't know the answer, say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm reading the question. It's long and is a little bit complicated. As was the case yesterday, I have not memorised the Dayton Agreement and I cannot tell you precisely, but I can make an informed guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not interested in an informed guess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking you because we believe that that should have been part of your work; albeit, you weren't asked directly by the Prosecutor. Incidentally, before embarking on your task, did you look at the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did look at the indictment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Saw who was indicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So you kind of understood from reading the indictment, and one does not need to be a legal scholar. Somebody with a Ph.D. from University of Indiana would be able to read it and know more or less the theory of the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I say that actually I'm not clear on the theory of the Prosecution case in this case, would that make me less than intelligent? I mean, I'm not a legal -- I am not a legal scholar. I did read the indictment, and I didn't consider it my business, really, to understand the direction. I was asked to do something and I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But why read the indictment if you didn't have to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was curious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were curious.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had time to kill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Then I take it, in performing your task here, you must have looked at the various implementation agreements, such as Geneva, Bonn, Rome, Sarajevo. These were all these agreements that took place between 1995 and 1996. Did you look at any of those, again all of them being available on the OHR, that's the Office of the High Representative web site? Did you look at that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have looked at most of those agreements in the same sense I have read the Dayton Peace Accords, but I did not memorise them and I did not consider them to be important in the preparation of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the answer is: Specifically, in this case, I did not look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You did not look at them as you were preparing for this report? Because I'm not asking you about memorising so you can tell us what's in them. As you can see, I'm not going through those documents, but I want to know whether you consulted those sources because they happen to be open sources available to the public. Did you look at them in preparation for your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like I said, I did not look at them specifically in preparation for this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now -- so -- and I take it if I were to ask you questions as: Have you read any of the expertise of the World Bank or the IMF in trying to build the economic system of the Federation of BiH, the answer to that would be "no" as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over time, I've read some of it, but I did not read it in preparation of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, who organized and who was responsible for the health care, for instance, in the Federation? You haven't read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many pension funds existed at the moment of the signing of the agreement of the Federation? That would have been 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, enough is enough. This is -- haven't we done enough since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your honour, this is my time. It is my time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is nothing more at this point than badgering the witness and I think out of mean-spiritedness. The witness has said repeatedly since yesterday that he did not need to nor did he look at the specific sources for this specific purposes, and to ask this witness in this context: "Do you know how many pension funds existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at a particular time," is irrelevant. It is completely irrelevant and is calculated only for the purpose of continuing to harass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be relevant. It may be relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It may be relevant if we're trying to discern, you know, the transitional process, and that's what I'm trying to do. Now, I can move on; but as the Prosecutor so eloquently pointed out, we need a record. And if I can quote him, you know, I'm entitled to make my record as well as he is, so I'm making my record. For instance, which enterprises provided electricity? That might be relevant at some point. How many intelligence organs or institutions existed at the signing of the Federation? How many existed at the signing of Dayton? How many existed thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That may or may not be the case, Your Honour. But at this point, everyone in the courtroom must know, I hope, that it's unfair to ask those questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on. If the Prosecutor is stating that he does not know, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas, we don't want to waste time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but also for the sake of the Defence, you wish to put questions and you know that the witness is going to say, "I don't know." So can you gather all these questions into one single question, and he'll be able to tell you: "I'm unable to answer," because he doesn't know about pension funds. And if you ask about power generating agencies after Dayton, he won't know. He doesn't know how officials are being paid. So I understood that you wished to develop your case, and to do so you wanted to put it on record. That's why you put the questions. Am I wrong or not about this approach of yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're -- well, you're not wrong, but there's a little bit more to that, Mr. President, because the -- with all due respect to what some -- some folks feel in this courtroom, I do think that the report is latent with value judgements that the gentleman made, which go to the line of the questioning. But in any event, I'll move on. I just have a couple of questions on that. I get your point and I'll move on, Mr. President. Two very quick questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have a budget for 1994 with all expenditure military police courts and education? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did Herceg-Bosna have a budget for 1994 with military police education expenditure? This is in 1994, so we're talking around Washington Agreement time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what positions Dr. Jadranko Prlic held as a result of the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Object to relevance, Your Honour. Again, I have no idea how this relates to whether Herceg-Bosna continued to exist or not, which again is the only question that was put to this witness. What positions Mr. Prlic held after this has no relevance to the question put to the -- the task put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. I'm going to answer your intervention, Mr. Scott. You surprise me somewhat, because in the documents that you had prepared in your binders, I can find the presidential minutes. Obviously, Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Prlic speak about the post-Washington period. These are documents provided by the Prosecution and the Defence knew about it. It is, therefore, only normal, maybe, that Mr. Karnavas should ask the witness whether he knows Mr. Prlic's position as to the outcome of the Washington Agreement. I'm somewhat surprised because this is to be found in the documents. There is one of them in which we see Mr. Prlic and Mr. Tudjman speaking about this very subject. So is the witness aware of this or not, I don't know. So please go ahead, Mr. Karnavas, with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apology for interrupting. Just to be clear, I'm not going to belabour it. I understand what the Court said. And it's certainly fair, absolutely fair, for Mr. Karnavas to ask about any document that specifically mentions Mr. Prlic's involvement such, for example, as the presidential transcripts, but I think the record will be very, very clear that I didn't ask about Mr. Prlic's positions or roles in terms of government after this time, nor do I think any of the documents get into that. But having said that, I want to make the record clear, but I understand your ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and it will become imminently clear to Mr. Scott where I'm going with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know his positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he served as prime minister or premier in the government of Herceg-Bosna. I believe he went on to serve as foreign minister of the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm asking you about the signing of the Washington Agreement, the formation of the Federation, pre-Dayton. Okay? So do you know what positions he held within the government - and I'm just using that term as we understand it - in BiH and any positions within the Federation in BiH as a result of the Washington Agreements? Do you know? It's a yes, no, I can take a wild guess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me go on to your report, the same report we were looking at yesterday. You indicate on page 1, at the very end: "Some of the ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the very last sentence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say: "Some of the more moderate Croats were dispatched to the Federation and state government, while many of the many more radical elements remained in place in Herceg-Bosna," and you cite some report which we know you looked at but didn't go into the basis of how they formulated those conclusions. Now, first of all, let's look at that. Who are the more moderate Bosnian Croats at this time that you're referring to, if you know; and if you don't know, just tell us, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm thinking of people like Kresimir Zubak, but I also believe that Prlic was dispatched or went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that word "dispatch." Thank you. Who dispatched him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who dispatched him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which authorities in Herceg-Bosna? So are you suggesting that somebody in Herceg-Bosna said: "Okay. Prlic, now, you're going to be a member of the Government of the Federation and of Bosnia-Herzegovina, while we hard-liners sit behind here in Mostar." Is that how -- how is it that you understand this? Because you, after all, are the historian and, we're talking about historical facts. And it would appear to me that there's some value judgements here, one of which I like because you're calling my client, you know, a moderate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would concede that there's a value judgement there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But ask me, where did you get this, where you say "dispatched"? If the answer is "I don't know," we can move on. Save yourself some time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said before, I accept the expertise of the people who prepared these reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: "Meetings of HDZ and local cantonal governors," et cetera, "serve as a real government of Herceg-Bosna where business is transacted." Now, I would assume that -- that for this particular comment, you must have looked at how the cantonal structures are vis-a-vis the Federation and what powers actually the cantonal governors had, right, or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll just repeat what I've said before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. We can save on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the answer wasn't I don't know. The answer was that I accept the expertise of the sources I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you concretely: And what if the source is wrong? What if? I know, as academics, we have to accept what other academics say; but from where I come from, at least, most academics a lot of times don't agree, especially historians, you know, and reasonable historians can reasonably disagree. So what if? And there's no footnote to this, by the way, there's a footnote following that, but I assume -- I'm going to take a wild guess that this is probably part and parcel of the same source. But what if they're wrong? You were asked to prepare a report. You didn't look what they were basing this on. You've already admitted to that. What if they're wrong? Then the answer would be: I don't know, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they're wrong, the answer would be that I used poor judgement in accepting the verdicts of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However, it sounds to me like you actually have been agreeing with the verdicts of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's go on to page 3, you say: "Croat leaders went further, even discouraging Croatian refugees and displaced persons from returning to areas now under the control of other ethnic groups." There's a footnote 9. Now, who are these Croat leaders? Name them in particular who were discouraging. And I would like to know, when you name a person, I want to know concrete facts, where you read it, not the report, but actual facts, because we know you haven't looked at the sources. So you're stating this, or is it the same answer: I've accepted what was in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Then you go on to say, the next paragraph, there are no footnotes, you say: "International organizations and other experts identified four sources of strengths and intransigence of Herceg-Bosna." First question: Is this a value judgement? Because earlier you want us to believe that you're just telling us the facts. Here it appears to be some sort of a value judgement, that there were intransigence. So, who are the international organizations? Do we know them? Because there's no footnote here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a concluding paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- excuse me. The value judgement, such as it is, is the value judgement of others. I'm simply reporting my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who are the other experts, other experts identified? So, if I want to go see these other experts, because maybe I want to challenge them as to this or maybe I want to have a discourse with them, maybe I want to be enlightened by them, who are these experts? Because they're unnamed here. Is it the same answer: It's a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say "international organizations and other experts," I'm simply concluding the past -- the section of the report. I'm referring to the people that I've cited, people and organizations that I've cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we go on to HDZ and Ante Jelavic. That section that starts on page 4. Now we're talking about HDZ. Now -- now here you say: "HDZ," in the first paragraph, "the HDZ split into two factions which divided along approximately the following lines: One headed by Ante Jelavic, Jadranko Prlic, and others, which continued to emphasise Herzegovinian interests, and second headed by Kresimir Zubak, which argued that they HDZ should consider the interests of Croats throughout Bosnia." Now, my first question is this: Is this a value judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't call that a value judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And where is it, based on what, because I don't see any information here, based on what are you saying that Jadranko Prlic was continuing to emphasise Herzegovinian interest? And before you answer that question, particularly, if you have not even bothered, you didn't even have the intellectual curiosity to find out what, if any, positions he held in the Federation and in the government of BiH at the time, based on what do you make this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This entire report is based on readily available second-source material. That will always be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, later on, you say that - I'm going to skip ahead a little bit - on page 5, you talk about a speech that Jelavic gave on March -- on 3 March 2001, and then you go on the following paragraph of -- you begin by stating: "While this rather convoluted formulation gave the appearance that HDZ still planned to work within the framework of Dayton, the party felt strongly that the election laws put Croats in Bosnia at the mercy of non-Croats." Now, is this a value judgement or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see it as a value judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You're just stating the facts? It's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm giving an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Giving an interpretation. Okay. Fair enough. Based on secondary sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No more than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know what was happening in Bosnia at the time and what exactly Mr. Jelavic was pursuing with respect to the rights of the Croatian nation within Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know what was the main gripe that he had and other Croats had within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The High Representative had moved to eliminate parties that he defined as nationalistic or extreme from political life in Bosnia, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that comes afterwards. Isn't it a fact that the Croats felt that they were disenfranchised, and that they in essence -- and I mean disenfranchised in the sense that by being part of the Federation, because of their numbers, that their national constitual rights were being jeopardized; isn't that the main thrust of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that that discussion is going on even today as the international community is attempting to find a solution to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And by the way, have you by any chance looked at the report for the Peace Implementation Council, that's Paris, France, December 14, 2005? It was authored by an R. Bruce Hitchner. He's from Tufts, Tufts University, and he is a member of the Secretariat of the Constitutional Working Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it you're not following what's going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Currently, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Would it surprise you if I were to tell you that the very same issues that the parties were discussing, in 1991, 1992, 1993, and onwards, are still being discussed today with certain -- with one -- with the Serbs, for instance, wanting to maintain the RS, the Bosniaks wanting more or less a unitary government, and the Croats trying to find a middle solution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, in this statement that this gentleman makes, this professor - he's a professor as well as you are - for the Croats whose demographic position in Bosnia is increasingly weak, the situation is no less difficult, as they must somehow, in the absence of their own entity, support a state government but is genuinely decentralised but at the same time functional and efficient. Isn't that, in essence, what Mr. Jelavic was pursuing at the time, or are you not able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that it's what he said he was pursuing, at the very least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at your first report. I don't know how much time I have left, but just very quickly, I just want to look at this first report. Again, when I look at it, I thought Mr. Murphy, who was also a professor here, was rather generous, when he said he would have given it a B minus, or you he would have given it a B minus. I would have given this a D plus to a graduate student, maybe a C to a freshman, but no more than that. This, again, this entire report is basically you having read certain newspaper articles and drawing some conclusions, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could put it that way I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I'm not going to go into the specifics, where you are lumping everybody as Yugoslav and what have you, but I do want to point out one thing. Let me get to this first. You indicate, at one page, you talk about the Graz negotiations; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, of course, somewhere in the paper, you do mention -- you do cite Burg and Shoup, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what is interesting is, because if we go on page 11 of your report, you say, at the bottom, right after footnote 33: "Speculation in Danas, the independent Croatian news weekly, could not compete with the concrete fact that Mate Boban and Radovan Karadzic actually negotiated as though the Croats did not exist in May 1992, one month into the war in Graz. The Graz negotiations resulted in the framework for these negotiations ..." And then you go on, and then you cite -- you say on the Graz negotiations, see so-and-so. That's the extent of your research on Graz, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the extent of my specific research on Graz for this paper, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, reading Shoup, and you say that this is a source that you use --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and you mention earlier -- on page 9, you mention a gentleman by the name of Adil Zulfikarpasic. I think anybody learning the language could pronounce that name because it has everything you need to know on pronunciation in B/C/S. You know who this gentleman is, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know he has a foundation in an extensive library or archive in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't have been able to be that specific but I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you quote him in November 1991. Now, in Shoup, on pages -- it starts with around 70 to 71, there's a long and drawn-out passage with respect to this gentleman with the SDS leadership going in August -- in July and August 1991, to Belgrade and trying to reach some sort of a secret negotiated deal where Shoup describes it. He says: "In effect, what began in 1991 as an effort to create a Greater Serbia by the Serbs in Croatia would then in this MBO," that's the party for this gentleman, "scenario be transformed into a greater Bosnia-Herzegovina," because earlier he's saying that, in a sense, the plan described Bosnia-Herzegovina not only as a republic but a state, "with a unitary government without regionalisation or cantonisation. All three provisions were absent in the Serb's draft," of course they're talking about. This called for autonomy, but it also called for, if the Serbs of Krajina left, they would also be part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, hence the Greater Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, I take it you take Mr. Shoup at his word, because that's what you indicated, one scholar must take another scholar at their word, that this actually was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He then goes on to say on page 73: "During the talks, on July 17, Adil Zulfikarpasic met with Milosevic in Belgrade. According to Zulfikarpasic's account, Milosevic threw his support behind the agreement. Upon his return to Sarajevo from the United States, Izetbegovic also visited Belgrade and conferred with Milosevic. Leaks of the conversation between Zulfikarpasic and Milosevic sent public opinion in Bosnian against the projected union in the prelude of the 'Belgrade initiative' came to naught. " And then it goes on to talk about what was reported in Borba and so on and so forth and a reaction from Mr. Kljuic, who obviously was not terribly pleased to hear about all this that was happening behind his back while he was in the government. Now, I take it again - and we'll bring this in through our case at some point - but, again, I mention all this because you indicated that one must take another scholar at their word. Tell me, you being the historian, was it not a fact that predating this statement by Zulfikarpasic, in November 1991, he along with Izetbegovic were courting Milosevic in order to stay in Yugoslavia, having secret negotiations. Was this not the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept that description, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And was there any reason why you did not bring out that, for balance sake, at least to say, there were secret negotiations from everybody on all sides and then cite Shoup, as you have, rather than to cite Zulfikarpasic to say that, in page 9, that a war would cause heavy casualties. Of course, that's a no-brainer. Everybody knows that. But why not say this very same gentleman, who was that concerned, was at the same time secretly negotiating with the Serbs? Why not put that in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could have put that in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't bother me to acknowledge that it could have been put in now, but I included the Zulfikarpasic quote because he specifically notes that a war would likely be a battle for destruction of one nation and clearing. So he was probably trying to avoid this outcome in his negotiations. I take it for granted that in most cites, that's what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And he's negotiating with Milosevic, "the prince of darkness of the Balkans."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is, and I agree with your value judgement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I mean, this is how he's been characterized. Whether he is or not, I don't know. But at this point in time everybody, says he's "the prince of darkness." So here we have Izetbegovic and this gentleman negotiating. Now, let me ask you this: Being a historian, knowing how the Croats felt, not just in Croatia, but also the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how do you think, or could you give us your expertise, how would they have reacted to that sort of a secret deal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just by point of clarification, is Mr. Karnavas suggesting that all Croats in Bosnia were one single mono-lithic group and that all Croats in Bosnia were to responded in the same way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, I said Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's first and foremost, and perhaps the gentleman would realise that there are two components to that country: Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My objection remains the same. All Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina have one mono-lithic response and position on these issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. I'll go back. I'll go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there any Croats in the government at the time back in 1991 in the Bosnia-Herzegovina government? And I'm saying "government" in the American sense, you know, like not just the prime ministerial and his cabinets, but were there Croats? Let me break it down any even further. Were there Croats in constituent nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to Yugoslav constitutional law --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say "Yugoslav" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- since we are talking about -- I mean, are we talking about before or after the war began?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm talking about before the war began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war had begun, in November of 1991 in Bosnia, the war had not yet begun. Croats were considered a constituent nation in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Bosnia, that's what I'm talking about. In Bosnia, itself, did Bosnia have a constitution as a republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It had a republican constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In transcript, it is missing a word of the gentleman. He said that Croats were considered people in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is not in the transcript. I just want to react on. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I need the help of my client, as you can see. Thank you, Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- all right. Now, how would the Croatian -- those who were in the government at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats, how would they have reacted to this secret negotiation? And if the reaction would have been benign, why have secret negotiations? Why not invite them in, since they're part of it -- since they are also a constituent nation? We more or less know where the Serbs are going. The Serbs in Bosnia want to be part of Yugoslavia. That's not a problem. So what do you think the reaction would have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I object to the relevance of this question. The first report was put -- the two questions that were addressed in the first report were quite clearly stated yesterday, and that was whether there were certain common features or practices about the conflicts, such as the mass displacement of people, ethnic violence, et cetera. And the second part, second question in the first report was to what extent that information was widely reported and known. And whether there were secret negotiations between the Muslims and with somebody else on a particular occasion, I don't see that has any relevance to the two questions the witness was asked to address. So we're once more into a situation where it's a free for all. It is an absolute free for all. There are no borders, there are no limits, there are no rules in the courtroom. It's just whatever Mr. Karnavas wants to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the topic is thinking about war in Bosnia. That's the topic that starts on page 8. Now, as I said, we have to put it into perspective. The problem with Mr. Scott, and I don't know where he's learned his trial skills from, but he can't just put a witness on direct and not expect the witness to be crossed. He can't open the door and as soon as I try to go in shut it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I expect him to be crossed on what he was asked to do and on the conclusions that he has reached, which he has clearly stated. I do not expect him -- I've been practicing law at least as long as Mr. Karnavas and at least as long as Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- excuse me, Your Honour, I will finish my statement, and that is that I expect the witness to be crossed appropriately. And the Chamber will note for the last 17 months I have rarely objected on cross-examination. I've given broad range. Only when I think it is, in fact, inappropriate and it's gone outside the scope are those times that I've objected, and this is one of those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the objection, the issue is as follows: Mr. Karnavas is asking the witness what or how would the Croats have reacted had they learned that there were secret negotiations going on in Belgrade between Milosevic and others, for example, Zulfikarpasic. We find this on page 9 of the report. That indicates that a Muslim political leader granted an interview in 1991, and so on and so forth. Hence, it would be interesting to know whether the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or had they learned of that, how would they have reacted. The witness may or may not know. So, Witness, what can you answer to the witness put by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm quite certain that they would have been upset, but I cannot give an yes or no answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't asking for an yes or no. This is where it's an open-ended question because it was outside the scope of direct examination in a sense, and that's why I wanted to give you full range, full depth and breadth to that answer. So can you expand on that, in particular because -- I want to address a little bit the Prosecution with this question. On page 6 you talk: "Yugoslavs," whoever they were, Yugoslavs, "were prepared for war in mid-1991, and the war they expected was an ethnic one." It's a wide-range statement. I assume that residents, citizens, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, irrespective of their creed or faith or nationality, are Yugoslavs, in a sense, because we still had Yugoslavia, that you're saying that they were preparing and expecting for war. So if they're there, if Izetbegovic is with Milosevic in July and August, secretly negotiating on carving up parts of Yugoslavia and what have you with these secret deals, would Izetbegovic and others know that this was likely to exacerbate the situation, cause fear and instability among the Croat population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the point they may think it might be necessary for them to self-organize themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this a wide-ranging question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a wide-ranging question. You go for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I suspect that the Croats in Bosnia could be expected to be upset upon hearing about such negotiations, but the historical context here - sorry, I'm talking too fast - but the historical context here is also important. Izetbegovic was undoubtedly negotiating with Milosevic because he understood that the Tudjman government had embraced a longer-term Croatian approach to Bosnia. The Croats had historically longed to incorporate significant parts of Bosnia into a Croatian state. Whether this is legitimate or not is not my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But this is present. This is something that all Yugoslavs had, - and they were Yugoslavs before the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I'm wondering about the tone of these remarks about my use of that term. And Yugoslavs, as a rule, understood that, you know, that the Croatian government had passed it, had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Pop quiz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pop quiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did Izetbegovic ever offer Herzegovina, for instance, to Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I seriously doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You seriously doubt it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You never heard of any offers made by Izetbegovic at any point in time to Tudjman that he can have Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, apparently you've run out of time; and as it is time for the break, please finish up quickly with one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I had it at the tip of my tongue. Give me a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you were talking about Tudjman, and you were talking about Izetbegovic having to go, like Oliver Twist sort of, to Milosevic, you know, with tin cup in hand, asking for protection. In essence, that's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But let me ask you this: Was the war waging on at this point in Croatia? Had it started there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the point that Izetbegovic spoke with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. We're talking about July, August 1991 when these secret negotiations are going on, had the JNA attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had begun.
