utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It had begun. Okay. And that's about the time, too, when these secret negotiations are going on and then Ravno is attacked, and Izetbegovic comes out and says: "This is not our war." This was the message to the residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which undoubtedly, as you must know, being a historian from a very fine university with a Ph.D., that the Croats took this to mean that this particular president is not looking at our best interests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a historian who has studied these questions deeper into the past than this trial is going into, I can tell you that it would be my highly educated guess that the Croats of Herzegovina were perfectly happy with that formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You mean with Croatia being attacked, Izetbegovic saying: "This is not our war," to a response to an attack on a Croatian village by the JNA, while the JNA is staging its attack against Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misunderstood, Mr. Karnavas, but it seems that at page 45, line 5, the witness says that, as a historian who has studied these questions deeply, more than this Court will do so, are you doubting that the Judges would look into it as closely as you would? I may have misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I would hope you would. But as I understand it, this trial is not -- is not about the historic Croatian attitude towards Herzegovina. I'm sure it's relevant. I meant no disrespect, but I've been getting a lot of comments in a relatively distasteful tone about my education, and so I thought I would just go ahead --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Be flip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and be flip right back to you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Let me break it down to you, sir. It's July/August 1991. By your own historical expertise, you indicated that Croatia has been attacked by the JNA. I mentioned Ravno, because as you might know or should know, Ravno was in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was attacked. You might also know that, at or about this time, the JNA was staging their attack against Croatia on the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that point in time, Izetbegovic is the president of the Presidency; but for all intents and purposes, he's acting like he is the president, not just first among equals, but above everyone else. At the same time, Izetbegovic is negotiating, either directly or through his proxies, with the Milosevic regime. And my question to you, sir, is very simple, okay: Would that -- given the circumstances at that point in time, is it surprising that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, realising what is happening and realising that after the attack on Ravno, Izetbegovic's best response is: "This is not our war" - and some have interpreted this mean that he's just going to sit on the fence - is it any surprise that the Croats felt insecure in their so-called leader, and as a result decided to self-manage in a sense and to begin to self-protect themselves? Is that -- is there any surprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to a couple of things. To the form of the question, it's a question that goes for, I don't know, some 20 lines of transcript. I'm not sure exactly what the question to the witness is at this point, number one. Number two, just so the record is clear, I think it would be more appropriate if Mr. Karnavas said the "alleged statement" by Izetbegovic, because there's other evidence before the Trial Chamber that that statement was never made. So it would be correct to say the "alleged statement" by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've never heard anybody disputing that statement, that's number one; and number two, while the question is rather long, you will note, Your Honours, that it's based on fact. It is based on evidence that has come before this Tribunal, and it's only at the very end where the question comes into play. All else is sort of the facts that have come through this court and are part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, go ahead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be happy to. I think that everybody in Bosnia had darn good reason to feel insecure at this point. I think Izetbegovic, if he actually made that comment, was making it out of a sense of profound insecurity, and I would not blame the concretes of Herzegovina for feeling insecure at this point either. It's a general phenomenon in Yugoslavia and its constituent parts at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I'm out of time, and we need to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is time to take the break, so we will now have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Defence, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to table a request, in view of your earlier guide-line, to allow my client Mr. Praljak to ask the witness questions directly, because I think that, in this specific case, it meets both conditions laid down in your ruling; that is to say, he has specific knowledge on the subject and directly participated in the events that the witness in the first part of his report addresses, and he sets out facts from which he draws conclusions. And along with this, one should bear in mind that, according to our position, expert testimony of this witness is not strictly historical. It oversteps the frameworks of historical expertise because it includes politicology as well and sociology, the sociology of society and enters into other fields of science and scholarly endeavour. I'd like to remind the court that Mr. Praljak, General Praljak was an active participant in the process of democratization in society at the end of the 1980s and beginning of 1990s, and they are topics which the expert witness touches upon in establishing certain facts that he sets out from. He studied sociology and philosophy and, therefore, is qualified, and he dealt with theory and practice and the literature as well and gained a knowledge of those subjects. And, in that sense, I think he meets both the criteria set out by you, and I, therefore, request that you allow General Praljak to ask his own questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would -- the Prosecution would object to Mr. Praljak's participation. This is -- to accept this kind of a showing as justifying his participation is a further illustration, with deep respect, that the limitations the Chamber has placed in implementation are meaningless, because there hasn't been -- I don't think there's been a topic yet on anything that the Chamber hasn't somehow viewed that he -- that it was relevant for Mr. Praljak to address it. So if that's the case, the limitations that the Chamber has implemented are meaningless. But, in any event, the Prosecution objects. This is material which all the other Defence counsel, Mr. Karnavas certainly demonstrated his ability to go through this material, and this is the classic kind of information material that any Defence counsel would be expected to go through, and we would object to Mr. Praljak's direct participation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Trial Chamber would like to ask you on what issues, on what points Mr. Praljak would like to ask the questions himself, on what elements with regard to which his knowledge of sociology, for example, would be useful? What topics would he address?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's a whole series of topics. Now, viewed realistically, Mr. Praljak won't be able to get through all those topics; but, for instance, he deals with Konrad Lorenz's well-known book "The So-called Evil." Now the witness ought to know this book and this literature, which directly enters into his conclusions with respect to his analysis and report, the first expert report which is titled: "The characteristics and patterns of the Balkan conflict as widely known and reported by the latter part of 1992." What I want to say is this: That part of the report by the witness, and yesterday we received certain explanations about this, is based on an assessment of certain sources quoted by the expert witness, upon which he relies in explaining the general characteristics and patterns of behaviour in the Balkan conflict, as is the title of his report. Now, it is our thesis that those weren't the sole factors, that's the first point; and, secondly, that it is open to discussion how far the press at the time that the witness relies upon viewed them correctly, because you needed a certain amount of knowledge beforehand in order to be able to view and understand the factors. And Praljak was involved in that process, the process before the conflict; that is to say, the democraticisation of society in 1989, when as single party system was abolished, and when suddenly, on the arena, we had new political forces appearing which were not organized, of course, although they existed. Now, he lived through this. He knew exactly what was happening. He knew what elements played a part and influenced events which later brought about direct conflict, or rather, the decisions on the part of Serbia and the Yugoslav People's Army to participate. Now, if you want to hear more in greater detail, General Praljak will be anticipate to go into this. I can do that myself, but I think that he will do it better, and we divided up the subjects that way. I prepared the second part of the report; that is, the time after the Washington Agreements and Dayton Agreements. So he would deal with the first part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, Mr. Kovacic. We have two reports before us, one of which relates to the period before the events in 1991 and 1992 for the most part, and the second report deals with what happened after the Washington Agreement. After the Washington Agreement, General Praljak no longer played any role, since upon returning to Croatia in November 1993, he apparently no longer played a role. On the other hand, with regard to his role prior to that, you say that he played a role in the process of democratization; in other words, everything that occurred before 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- or, Your Honour, you noted that very rightly. Now, in this second expert report, that is to say, events after Dayton, Mr. Praljak has not prepared any questions on that part of the report. I will be doing that part. But as my colleague has covered that, I don't want to go into those matters and I would rather leave time, more time, to General Praljak. But everything in 1990 and 1991, which is what the witness begins with, his first chapter until June 1991, he lays down some premises as to the context of why events developed as they did subsequently. It was in that area that Praljak took an active part. That is the time when the parties began to be formed. That is the time when democratic pound [as interpreted] authority began to be established, and Praljak really was involved in all those events fully. He devoted all his energy and time into that process, and nobody knows about these events better than he.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, he played a role in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatia in 1989, 1990, and 1991, in Croatia, and this entire story or presentation by the expert witness begins, as you yourselves were able to see, with that period. And he says that certain general characteristics and patterns of the Balkan conflict began to become manifest, according to what the expert witness says, in those first events in Croatia. And so the first chapter takes us up to June 1991. So that's the basic thesis laid down by the expert witness, and then those same patterns, ethnic persecution, and so on and so forth, were reflected in Bosnia. And by the sake token, any reasonable man, if we were to look at the positions in Bosnia in 1991, should have known that this was the template for what happened in Croatia. And it is our thesis that General Praljak can explain this to you, that he himself devoted his full time and energy and knowledge and participated precisely in the creation of these new conditions, the aim of which was to democratize society. And this democratization was opposed by certain forces, and that's what brought about the war ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I interrupted you. You wanted to still add something? What more did you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say and to round off with the last sentence. Those are the circumstances. Those are the precise circumstances which the witness selectively addresses. He selects these various circumstances to put forward his thesis, and his main source was several newspapers. Quite obviously, this didn't take place in a sterile environment. Everything that took place needs the knowledge of society, and we know it was a multitude of factors which were at play here and which we should take into consideration far more facts, put them on the table in order to assess the reality. Praljak took part personally in this process, and let me also add that he really does have specific knowledge, not only formal education and having studied sociology and philosophy, but he has general social knowledge. And I must repeat, the analysis, the report, and the knowledge of the author, at the least he needs is historical knowledge, because a lot of these things are politicological information and sociology of society. That's what makes this analysis or report the kind of material that we can address, and I think that that's why we must show that, presented in this way, it merits questions in the way I have described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Judges have debated the point and allow Mr. Praljak to ask questions solely with regard to the period that goes up to April 1992, where it starts with the war in Croatia, and not regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina, so solely with regard to the events in Croatia in 1990, 1991, up to April 1992 because Mr. Praljak was at the time in Croatia. So that is to be the scope of our leave to Mr. Praljak. So, Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. And with regard to time, Mr. Praljak has 30 minutes, is that right, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he was given some time from some of the other Defence teams. I was doing other business, so he'll tell you himself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I have been given ten or 15 minutes from the -- from Mrs. Alaburic. I will adhere to your instructions. I didn't intend to deal with the part that Mr. Karnavas has already dealt with, but I'm going to deal with facts, facts on the basis of which value judgements are being made. Cross-examination by Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Tell me, to start off, which historical evaluation is not a value judgement? Is there any historical judgement which is not, in fact, a value judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that we're, once again, I guess getting into definitions of value judgement. But for me, a value judgement is a judgement that I make when I apply my values to you and your situation, and probably avoid a reckoning with the facts. I think, though, you know, any historical evaluation is going to be an interpretation, and I suppose it would be open to the accusation that value judgements are involved. We historians argue and debate the merits of various interpretations all the time, and sometimes I think we would conclude that more or less value judgement is involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we'll skip over that. You say you read the paper Danas, the Croatian journal, and the Hrvatski Tjednik, the other journal. Now, can you tell me, please, whether you read the Vecernji List, Vjesnik, Slobodna Dalmacija, Rijecki Novi List, Osijecki Glasnik, Glas Slavonije? Have you read those papers? Did you read those papers in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my professional life, I have read Vecernji List I have I have read Slobodna Delmacija. I have occasionally read Glas Slavonije. I did not read the newspapers in the preparation of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, of the weeklies, Globus, Nedjeljna Dalmacija, and Hrvatsko Slovo, did you read those weeklies in preparation for this trial? Did you use that as a source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Realtime transcript read in error "No"].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you read Danas, do you know the circulation that it was published in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to say that I didn't say "no" to that previous question. I don't know if I made a noise or something, but I did look at Globus, but I didn't use it in the report. So, okay. No. I couldn't tell you the circulation numbers for Danas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell me the name of a single newspaper [as interpreted] who worked in the weekly Danas who was not a prominent member of the League of Communists beforehand -- a single journalist or newspaperman who cooperated and wrote for Danas who had not been a prominent member of the League of Communists of Croatia for many years beforehand? Can you quote me a single name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, sorry. I really do not see the relevance of your question. Of course, we know that in that time in Yugoslavia, like in all other former communist countries, there had been communists in everywhere. So, frankly, I do not know what is the relevance of your question. You had already raised this question before, beforehand, but I do not think it is a question which should be asked from the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Prandler, the relevance of the question is the following: The communists were still, and particularly around the newspaper Danas - I can't go into that today - but they still supported the thesis that Yugoslavia was tenable, and, therefore, their reports were -- quite lacked objectivity or were so far away from objectivity that they supported an idea that was disintegrating and falling apart. So that's why I'm asking him whether these journalists were members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia beforehand, or did they belong to the particularistic nationalists. I asked about that but the gentleman didn't know. I think the question is a relevant one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Praljak. I understand your arguments. On the other hand, if I'm not mistaken, and if I do recall, you have written your doctorate thesis at the university about the Marxist ethics. So in this case, is it so -- Marxist ethics. So, I believe that this issue of always speaking about former and other communist cities, frankly, it is not within the scope of the indictment. It is not within the scope of the reports, what the gentleman has written. So, therefore, I do insist that you are asking questions which are related to the report. The Chamber decided that your questions should be in a way to be put on the two parts of the report, that is, before June 1991 and the beginning of the war in Croatia, and nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could join Judge Prandler's objection. The Prosecution makes the same objection to the relevance. This question when asked, and again I'm looking at the first report, when asked which of the conclusions, which of the conclusions in the first report with the fact that some of the writers were communist have any impact, how would that change? How does that draw into question the conclusions reached by this witness, and there's one example only, just one example. On page 7, for example, at the top, he makes reference, as we discussed on Monday, to the killing of -- the killing of civilians that they were forced to walk for a minefield in October 1991, that were forced by Serb -- Serb forces to do that. Now, is Mr. Praljak saying that because there could have been some of the people who wrote some of these things were communist that that event didn't take place? So what is it exactly? How is this exactly relevant to the question of -- to the questions, to the conclusions reached by this witness? I don't see any relevance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please go on. By asking this question, did you want to imply that the journalists of Danas, according to you, were members of the communist party and, hence, were in favour of maintaining Yugoslavia? Well, if so you've said it, now please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, all I want to do is to ask one thing, and that's why I quoted all the papers or a large number of them. Did the witness objectively, which is the duty of a historian, write about this? He writes about the sources. I didn't mean to denigrate the people in Danas, but I just wanted to show that the witness in his selection kept one side, regardless -- I didn't want to go into whether they were objective or not. I just wanted to demonstrate that his sources were not diverse but just one-sided sources. So that's what I wanted to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you deal with the Balkans; and before this trial, I wrote a book and I'm going to go through the history of Yugoslavia briefly. Tell me, please, between 150 and 200.000 Croats, were they killed in Blajburg in Slovenia after World War II and along the Roads of the Cross? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you also know that after this war, in free Slovenia, 410 graves were found, 298 mass graves, 87 pits, 15 anti-tank trenches, six mines, and four anti-aircraft shelters, in which mostly the Croats who were killed and withdrew in face of the Allied forces were buried there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, would you be so kind to explain to us how this relates to this first report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, the witness states quite clearly in his report that the whole problem of a multi-national society in Yugoslavia begins -- began with Tito's death, and that that Yugoslavia, a good Yugoslavia, which we can deduce from his reform, were toppled by national particularism. So everything was all right and hunky-dory up until then, he says. The League of Communists was a wonderful organization; and because Tito did not provide an heir, just as if it were perhaps the Habsburg Monarchy, or whatever, and because some bad nationalists wished to break up the Yugoslavia, as it existed, the following evil ensued. So I want to show through my questions on the basis of which Yugoslavia was formed, what was the essence of the communist regime, and what evils it lived within it by quoting figures. I was just quoting figures here to demonstrate that, from the very beginning, it was prison, and that there were desire for democracy throughout and that no particularistic nationalism toppled the country, but that it was toppled as a dictatorship. So I would like to quote a few more examples, if that is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: In my view, it is not all right. Please proceed with the relevant chapters of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Trial Chamber has already taken a unanimous decision, requesting that you focus on the period from 1990 to April 1992 and events in Croatia. In your previous questions, you've raised other issues. My colleague feels that it is not relevant. Personally, I would have been interested in hearing your questions, but I will agree with the other Judges, respect their opinion. I imagine that you will be able to ask these questions through other witnesses, since they seem important to you. This witness has only talked about 1990, 1991, and 1992, so please limit your questions to that period; otherwise, the scope will be entirely different. It is certainly of interest as well; but with regard to this witness, it may seem less relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but I don't know how we're to understand the thesis, it is a thesis, that the Yugoslav elite -- on page 2 of the gentleman's report, that the Yugoslav elite stood behind the particularistic type of nationalism that had always existed side by side with the Yugoslav idea. So in what way - and I'm talking to historian dealing with the Balkans - can we start up the decision at a time when the country is disintegrating. It is the disintegration of a society which -- and they were led throughout a period of 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Explain to me, please, sir, why did Yugoslavia disintegrate, because of particularist nationalisms, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a question before I answer -- never mind. It disintegrated because it was led by a dictator from 1944 to 1980, who approached the country as a series of people all possessing nationalisms that needed to be crushed in order for stability to be maintained. Nothing in my report ever intimated that I thought Tito was a good person; but when he died, there was nobody in a position to continue those repressive policies. His enforced Yugoslavism - I'm trying to be as clear as possible here - his enforced Yugoslavism failed to be sustained thereafter; and, instead, these words particularist nationalisms are not mine. That's not to say I'm distancing myself from them. That's not my choice of words. But the those particularist nationalisms filled the vacuum. I have no value judgement on this. The dictator, nationalisms, neither sides evokes any feeling in me. I think it was -- the nationalisms themselves increased in-- they were more vital. They became more aggressive and ultimately more violent, thanks to the fact that they had been actively repressed after 1944. I hope that answers your question, but I would be happy to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. In part, it does. What about the desire for freedom, for liberty, for democracy? What about the American Declaration of Independence and the right enshrined in that declaration which you believe in and advocate? What about the rights of nations? Did the USSR fall apart because of nationalisms? Did the whole system crumble because of nationalism, or was it because of the desire for freedom, liberty, democracy, the rights of nations and so on and so forth, as set out in the American Declaration of Independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could debate the nature of the Declaration of Independence and our Constitution for a long, long time, but I don't believe that the rights of nations are enumerated in those documents. I think the rights as citizens as individual are, but that's just me. I think the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia fell apart for basically the same reason, and that is that they were or had been dictatorships. They couldn't sustain themselves. Third point, I think that very often nationalism is, in fact, an expression for a desire of freedom. But I think, unfortunately, that it, ultimately, very often lapses into a desire for freedom in a sort of zero-sum gain, where one nation's freedom means another's lack of freedom. In a case of a country like Yugoslavia, where territories were I think factually nationally mixed to a great degree, one man's expression of nationalism is going to be another man's expression of oppression in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the following now: Referring to Yugoslavia, was the full name of the country, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Therefore, I won't go into legal issues, but are you aware that nowhere in Yugoslavia, except for Brezhnev's Doctrine, is the principle of the right of nations to self-determination, going as far as secession limited -- that was Lenin's principle, guaranteeing the right of nations to self-determination going as far as secession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware that that right is in the 1974 Constitution of Yugoslavia. The reference to the Brezhnev Doctrine is lost on me. Nonetheless, the right to the self-determination of nations, as opposed to republics, is a complicated issue; and since no nation inhabited only a single republic and alone, this is not quite as simple in practice as it is in constitutional form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When referring to republics and nations, can you quote the first three sentences of the socialist constitution of -- the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia? What did the first three sentences say? Or if you cannot recall, do they say the following: "The Croatian state is the national state of the Croatian nation. Croatia is the country of the Serbs and the other nationalities living in it." Are these the opening sentences, the first sentences, of that constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not memorised them, but that does sound like -- I know that there's a distinction between the socialist versus the constitution that came into effect in 1991, and that sounds to me to be an accurate rendition. I accept your word on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is -- are you serious, Mr. Praljak? "The Croatian state is a national state of the Croatian nation. Croatia is the country of the Serbs and the other nationalities"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it correctly. I'm sure of what I'm saying because it's something I have dealt with for 40 years. "Croatia is the state -- is a state. Croatian is the national state of the Croatian people. Croatia is the state of the Serbs and other nations and nationalities living in it." That's what the first three sentences of the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia say. The reason I'm saying it is that the witness, in his report, says that by changes of the constitution when Croatia gained independence, the Serbs became second-class citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In what sense, in what way, Witness, do you say that the Serbs became second-class citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the precise language that was used, and I would readily admit that the difference between the constitutions would seem kind of arcane and inscrutable to outsiders, that the language that was used in the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, after Franjo Tudjman came to power, clearly offended the Serbian population of Croatia, even if to an outsider it's difficult to understand why. And I do not remember the precise language, but I'm -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you don't know what it said exactly, how can you assert that something can offend someone? Please look in my bundle of documents and look at document number 3D01085. 3D01085. That is a document published by the Croatian parliament on the 8th of September, 1991, breaking off state links with the -- with Yugoslavia after the expiry of the moratorium that had been imposed after the Brioni Declaration and after the Serb air force bombed the building of the cabinet and Presidency of the Republic of Croatia, the so-called Banski Dvori. Are you aware that that happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please read point 5 or paragraph 5: "The Republic of Croatia, as a sovereign and independent state, by guaranteeing and safe-guarding fundamental human rights and the human rights of national minorities, guaranteed explicitly in the United Nations Universal Declaration, the Helsinki Summit Final Act, OSCE documents," and so on and so forth. Who can be offended by such a position if they wish to be a citizen of a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me to speak for the Serbian population of Croatia, but I can tell you what offended them, the fact -- no --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I thought you were telling me to stop. They were offended by the fact that Serbs weren't explicitly listed, and they were offended by the fact they were designated a national minority. Me, that wouldn't cause me to rebel; but, I suppose, in historical Croatian conditions, that was considered a dangerous precedent by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you have read the memorandum of the Serb Academy of Arts and Sciences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read it through and through, and I've written about it and yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that a clear political standpoint of the Serbian intellectual elite to the effect that they want all Serbs, regardless of republican borders, to live in a single state? Is that clearly stated there, either explicitly or implicitly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's implicit in the document; it is not stated explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, within the scope of this, did Milosevic conduct his entire policy in such a way that he suspended the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia by abolishing two provinces: Kosovo and Vojvodina, doing this on his own and without consulting the other republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to read your comment here. In 1988 and 1989, he did, in fact, suspend the constitution of -- or, excuse me, he did change the constitutional status of Kosovo, Vojvodina, and the -- he did impose a leadership in Montenegro that was friendly to him. I'm not sure I would go so far as to say this was done with the sort of authority of the memorandum which actually had no authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing. Within the framework of this kind of national project with Milosevic at its head, did the Yugoslav People's Army, a few years before the war, reorganise itself in such a way as to safeguard the borders of a Greater Serbia Karlovac-Ogulin-Virovitica line in Croatia, that line, that axis, in Croatia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that that line has a deeper history in Serbian politics, and I take the word of scholars who are better-informed on these issues that the Yugoslav People's Army did, in fact, reposition its units to defend a Serbian state. And by "line," I'm referring to that Karlovac-Ogulin-Virovitica line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please look at 3D01086, 3D01086: Pursuant to requests by the Badinter Commission that before recognition, the republics have to conduct a referendum as to whether their citizens want a state, on the 29th of April and on the 19th -- proposed and on the 19th of May, 1991, there was a referendum held at which there were two possible questions: One, the Republic of Croatia, as a sovereign and independent state, guaranteeing the cultural autonomy, as well as all rights to the Serbs, so the Serbs are mentioned here, and other nationalities in Croatia may join an alliance of sovereign states with other republics; and second, the Republic of Croatia remains a part of Yugoslavia as a single federal state. Are you aware that these two questions were put at the referendum pursuant to the request of the Badinter Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if there are no deeper reasons of conquest on the territories of Slovenia and Croatia within the project of a Greater Serbia, who can be offended by a question formulated in this way and why would they be offended by it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, once again, I can't speak for Serbs. I mean, I guess I can understand historically their reluctance to trust the Croatian government. Croatia had a 20th century history of a series of events in which they mistreated the Serbs of Croatia and Bosnia. I'm sure the independent state of Croatia is familiar to us all. So I think anything that didn't explicitly guarantee the rights of Serbs, as such, was going to be taken, let me put it this way, could potentially be taken as inflammatory and could be used in a propagandistic sense by more extremist Serbs in Croatia. No value judgement intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot -- but anyway. To what extent did Chetnik crimes against Croats and Muslims in World War II in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- do you know how many Muslims and Croats were killed by Chetniks in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in World War II? Because you've mentioned the guilt of Pavelic's state. What about Nedic's state and Draza Mihajlovic's Chetniks? Both were criminals. But what was the ratio of crimes? What was the proportion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the ratio of crimes. I'm inferring from this that I'm being asked to compare relative guilt or merits of the two peoples in the Second World War and after, and I just simply can't. But from the Serbian perspective, Croatia was a dangerous place. If the Croatian perspective was that Serbs were dangerous and being unified with a Serbian-dominated state was dangerous, I would understand that as well. But I don't know the numbers, and I know that they're heavily disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. We will have other witness to deal with this information. Are you aware from your research that the independent state of Croatia and the fascist regime of Ante Pavelic have been criminalised to a far greater extent than Nedic's fascist regime, which was in power in Serbia and committed the same crimes and the Chetniks of Draza Mihajlovic? Have you reached that conclusion in your research?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Prosecutor, I'm referring to fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tried not to interrupt and I suppose Mr. Praljak can waste his time any way he wishes, but, again, I thought the Chamber's instructions was to address the period 1990 to 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Actually, I would like to say the same, that we have already asked Mr. Praljak to speak about that particular period of time. I could also go into terrible details which happened during the Second World War. Hungarian's killed a number of people, but our neighbors killed a lot of Hungarians. And after this, frankly, it doesn't make too much sense now to repeat all those things. Actually, Mr. Praljak, you have already asked about these questions during the last 17 months at least five or six times. So please understand, we do not want to prevent you to ask questions, but we have actually given to you rather clear instructions that you have to reflect about those parts of the report which are there before you and those two parts which you would like to ask -- which we would like you to ask questions. Please kindly accept this ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept this, Your Honour, but the witness started speaking about the fear of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please look at 3D01081, and we'll move on quickly. Please look at the document. It's an assessment of war damages in Croatia. Did you in any way deal with the available sources as to the extent of war damage in Croatia because of the aggression by the JNA and the rebel Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their Honours may keep this document if they wish. Calculations may differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But would you agree that in total the damage can amount to $252 billion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have absolutely to idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please look at document 3D01076. Are you aware that on the current territory of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may assist the witness, it is a separate book by the bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the present-day territory of Republika Srpska about 700 Catholic churches or church buildings have been destroyed, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that particular number. I'm aware of massive destruction of religious institutions and churches and parishes throughout the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you aware that within the borders of present-day Republika Srpska, more than 200.000 Croats have been expelled who have never been able to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not aware of particular numbers, but I'm aware of the phenomenon and I don't dispute the enormity of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Look at 3D01074. Are you aware that only in those 11 municipalities I dealt with in Republika Srpska in the course of 1991 and 1992 and also part of 1993, 840 Croats were killed? Are you aware of this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not. Of course, I'm aware that Croats were killed in the Republika Srpska, but the precise number I wouldn't have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, again, could you tie this to the witness's report in some way? I do not quite see the relevance of the question and the relation,-- except that it's the tu quoque argument that we often hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours. No, no. I have distanced myself a hundred times from that. This is a witness who is a historian, and Your Honours who are lawyers. Not for a moment did I think that everyone who has committed a crime should not be tried. We are speaking about cause and effect here. It's about who started the chaos, who did the killing, who did the destruction, and what the repercussions were in society. It's impossible to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I did not read the report as being a report which tries to find out who started the war. That was not my reading of this text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please look at the report. Nowhere is the word "aggression" mentioned at all. There are three sides mentioned here without beginning and without end. Three sides committing crimes, yes, that's true. But here there is -- it says: "Tudjman's government tried to take Knin as an SDS stronghold in order to prevent the referendum."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Witness, please, when and with what did Tudjman's government want to take Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... with men who had guns. I honestly don't know. Knin was part of the Republic of Croatia. They were trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How can the police of the Republic of Croatia sending two helicopters to retake a police station taken by rebels and JNA planes on the territory of the Republic of Croatia force these helicopters to turn back, which is a coup d'etat, and you say quite coolly that Tudjman's government tried to take Knin as an SDS stronghold. Knin was full of logs. It had been taken by rebels in the then-still socialist state, which was a regular state, a regular republic. Explain that to the Judges. That's why I'm putting these questions, or if you have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a long comment. I would be happy to give you a shorter answer. You know, it's a matter of perspective, obviously, that the SDS and its leadership had, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the Judges won't let me speak about perspective, so don't you talk about perspective either. If I can talk about perspective, then we'll talk about psycho-analysis and socio-psychopathology, and sociology, but that is not our historical task. Your historical task here is to establish whether Knin, the police station in Knin, was in Croatia and whether it had been occupied by rebels headed by Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in Croatia, it had been occupied by rebels, I agree with that formulation, and it was retaken or the attempt was made to retake it by the Croatian government. And I don't actually see how that differs from what I said in my report, but be that as it may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But where, where in your report does it say the rebels had taken, in a regular republic part of a federal state the rebels, had taken a police station? What country in the world would not send its regular policemen to take it back within the constitutional order? But where do you say this? Let's move on. On the same page, page 3, you say that the taking of police station in Pakrac, and you say here "by Serb rebels" and so on. And you say that in Pakrac the Serbs accounted for 38 per cent of the population, 30 per cent was accounted for by the Croats, and 21 per cent was made up of Yugoslavs. We can put that on the ELMO, but I will read it. According to the census of 1991 in Pakrac, there were 27.509 inhabitants and the ratio of Serbs and Croats corresponds to what you say, but there were 71 -- 718 Czechs, 273 Hungarians, there were Slovaks, there were 860 Italians, 330 -- 46 Yugoslavs. So how can you say that there were 21 per cent Yugoslavs, that's my first question; and secondly, what happened to the Hungarians, Slovaks, and Italians after the Serbs occupied Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was quoting a source which I considered and still consider to be reliable, and I'm afraid I have no idea what happened to those poor people who were caught in the middle of an argument that was not theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the attack on Vukovar, can that be played and can we see what that looked like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I need to do something? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Under fire, civilians were still coming out of their cellars. It seems that not all the Croatian soldiers had surrendered. The federal army and Serbian irregulars were dealing with them. "The Serbs were celebrating in the streets that they had fought for. The aftermath of battle lay everywhere and, inevitably, there were charges of atrocities impossible to confirm on the ground. The regular army has acted with restraint, and it was the army this afternoon which secured the former Croatian police station and moved to the hospital next to it. There hundreds of casualties are waiting for evacuation. Vukovar's ordeal is still not over. "Martin Bell, BBC news, Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, the attack on Vukovar, was it an aggression, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, after the 1.800 fighters of the Croatian army who fought there in those units, were there a hundred Serbs according to your information or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From that town, were 10.000 people taken away to camps in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know precise numbers about -- on these two issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many bodies who have still not be found are still sought and looked for by the Republic of Croatia of people who disappeared from Vukovar? Is it in the hundreds, the thousands, or what, after all the peace conferences and humanistic declarations made those bodies are still being searched for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the numbers are of people who are still missing from Vukovar. I imagine it's a very high number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that in the town of Osijek more than 700 civilians were killed when the Serbian artillery fired, to the best of your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Slav -- in the Slavonia subregion, Bosnian artillery, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't they kill more than 500 civilians and a large number of children within that number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not be surprised, but I do not know specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The UNPA zones that were set up in Croatia, four of them, under the protectorate of the United Nations, while it was under UN control, according to your information, were more than 600 Croatian civilians killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I don't know and I'm not going to know specific numbers about any of these cases. I must as well specify that right now. I don't doubt your numbers; I just don't know that they're accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to wind up with exercise in simulation, 3d01077 is the next piece of exhibit. Now, France, I have interpolated where Croatia would be and I put the population of France and its surface area there; and then on the second page, I do this for Croatia. I put it in place of Croatia; then on page 3, the attack by the Yugoslav Army forces from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Serbia. You can look through that, then we have occupied territory. Is it true that a third of Croatia was occupied in 1991, 1992, 1993, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we all know the figures for the displaced persons and refugees in the Republic of Croatia; and if I translated that in terms of the population of France, would you agree that Croatia, in the course of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, had 800.000 and more than that displaced persons and refugees from Croatia and from Bosnia-Herzegovina? You could see that in the Mazowiecki reports and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm having a little bit of trouble following the question. I'm not sure what,"if I translated that in terms of the population of France" means, but I think I agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the number of Croats, 4.200.000, for that period of time, I tried to depict this as happening in France, which means that Frenchmen expelled from France would be 2.800.000, the ratio, displaced persons two and a half million killed, 151.000 wounded, 351.000, those who died for unknown reasons 10.000, and so on. So I calculated the ratio. Now, you can skip a page and look at 1992 to see what happened after the Serb invasion, what was left of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the BH army and the HVO where together, that was the white part, and the rest of France which we superimposed on Croatia the territory of Croatia. Now, the in view of the fact that you dealt with Karadjordjevo, tell me this, please, from France, this kind of France, or you can read that as Croatia, you can divide Croatia from Bosnia-Herzegovina along the Karlovac-Karlobad-Ogulin line, how does that correspond with the agreement made in Karadjordjevo between Tudjman and Milosevic, the alleged agreement about the carving up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They allegedly reached some agreement on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I'm not clear on this in view of the clearly declared Serb aspirations. Where could the borders of such a state be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I object to not being able to understand the question. I have no idea what the witness has been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, be more specific in your question because we're somewhat lost. Please rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if it was the Serbian desire and they had taken over a third of Croatian territory to have the Karlobag border line, et cetera, then where would that state border on any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would belong to Croatia, according to alleged agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic? I don't know if I've made my question any clearer now. Well, you needn't answer that. It will be self-evident from the maps we're going to show, but now let's look at the last map, registered and recorded displaced persons in France. And after this, we have the displaced persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the same ratio, and we're dealing with 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996. Now could you tell me the following. Is it correct that Croatia, in 1990 and 1991, A, was it attacked? Is that correct? Was Croatia attacked? That's my first point and question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to admit, I'm confused, too. But if I'm taking that question in isolation, I would argue that there are two ways of looking - I'm sorry, I won't use the P word, the perspective word - but I think there are two ways of looking at what happened in Croatia in 1991. It, obviously, objectively seceded from Yugoslavia and then the Yugoslav Army, in fact, did attack it, but I'm still a little confused about the relationship to the simulations we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. We can forget simulation for the moment. But you're denying the right. According to the constitution, the right exists of a federal unit, pursuant to the constitution which was in existence on the Lenin principle, has the right to self-determination to the level of secession. So do you deny the republic the right that it cannot secede from a country that it no longer wishes to belong to? Is that your thesis? Is that what you want to say? So if it wishes to secede and separate it, then somebody else has the right to attack it. Is that what you're saying? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I neither deny nor advocate any of it. I have no horse in this race. I try to describe it in a rational way and sometimes I can't even do that, but, simply, I am not denying or advocating a thing. I try to describe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm really sorry. This is the third time I have to ask you to try to concentrate on the report, and here you have the report before you and everybody has it. And here you are concentrating to the period of time, which is in that report, in the chapter, and I quote, "from June 1991 to April 1992, war in Croatia." And it starts at page 3, and it goes on actually until page 8. And at page 8, you will find a new chapter to start, Thinking about war in Bosnia. Now, we have heard, again, a number of crimes about -- a number of crimes, about the number of those who were killed, et cetera. It is very regrettable, but I would like you to really concentrate on pages 3 and 8, and to tell us and to tell the witness or ask the witness about it, if you disagree with his findings in this chapter. And it is what we are talking about. It is a cross-examination of the witness about his report and reports. So, again, I would like to plead with you that we have already heard, during the last couple of months, a number of times, a great number of times, about the same very regrettable facts. And we do not want to in a way to close our eyes before those facts; but, on the other hand, we do have here a witness who wrote a particular report. He should be asked about his report and not to recapitulate everything which we have already heard about the war in Croatia and in other places. And really believe me that it is a counter-productive if you are doing this, I have to tell you frankly. Sometimes too much is worse than something not so much but very well-based and in a way very to the point. But what you are doing is overkill and figuratively speaking, and I ask you to restrain yourself on that very issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Judge Prandler, but I cannot agree with that. I'm just asking the following question. On page 4 the witness says: "Borovo Selo was a Serbian village, while Borovo Naselje was mostly Croatian."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that Croatian territory or Serb territory as a whole, Witness, Mr. Historian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it wasn't Serbian. It was a village in which the majority population was Croatian and Serbian. So the precision of the historian's declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I just wanted to say three things and ask three things: Was Croatia attacked? Did Croatia change its political system? And at that point in time, was Croatia creating its own state? Did it take in 800.000 refugees? How many wounded did it have? And what was the situation in the rest of the country where the whole infrastructure was destroyed, and I'm comparing data for you to gain a picture of what was happening. Of course, I cannot speak of Konrad Lorenz and the production of "Evil" and all the rest of it, and what kind of control was possible. Quite simply, we have to have historical comparisons, and here we have a historian who is able to do that. I don't have any more questions on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just confirm this for me, did Croatia move from a dictatorship, as you say, to a democracy, and was it creating a state of its own, which it did not previously in that form, and was it attacked by an all-out aggression with the army putting it into place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was doing the first two things you mentioned; and on the third I suppose, there are nuances that I would dispute with you, but there's no question that war was the result. And, in fact, the point of my report is that everybody knew it, and everybody knew what the nature of that conflict was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Praljak. Well, you've used up already 45 minutes. You had 30 minutes initially, with another 15 minutes coming from Mr. Petkovic. We'll now have a break, so please finish with your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've already asked my last question. I just want to say that when I was one of the leaders of the rebellion against the authorities at the time, that is to say, in the 1960s, I took part in the democratic transformation of society, and I have a lot of knowledge about facts, about society, language, culture, everything that makes up a nation. And every war is forged in peace when basic prerequisites are denied, the prerequisites of ethnicity and something we call nation, nationality, or ethnicity. So we won't be able to get at the cause of this war, because then afterwards it appears that everybody attacked everybody else, that everybody was offended and insulted, now which nation was pilfered, how many people were killed, civilians incarcerated, and so on and so forth; and then somebody seems to be insulted or offended because he wasn't set apart or was set apart by a constitution. We have to deal with all those matters here. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we've done an estimate of the time. Ms. Alaburic had given 15 minutes to Mr. Praljak, therefore, the Petkovic Defence will have 15 minutes. I can't remember what happened to Mr. Stojic. Mr. Murphy, did you give us your time estimate or not? I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think I'll be just five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon to all my colleagues in the courtroom. If I need a little time, and I think I will need only five to ten minutes to complete what I intended to talk about with this witness, my colleague Mr. Murphy will give me the time I need, so I ask Your Honours to bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, I will speak to you exclusively about your first expert report, and I wish to put a few questions to you, which I believe might assist Their Honours in issuing a decision as to whether this expert report should be admitted into the evidence as relevant to our case. So to begin with, can we agree on the aim of your report. If I understood it correctly, you wish to show that there were generally known characteristics of the conflict on the former -- on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, which was an ethnic conflict, and that violence against civilians belonging to a different ethnic group was in a certain way an integral part of the conflict? Did I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In other words, you wished to show that, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, everybody knew what the nature of the conflicts were which took place in the early 1990s. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just since the Prosecution is the one that set the questions, I just wanted to be clear that he was not asked to show something. He was asked to investigate a question and whether or not what the nature of the conflict was. He was not given a mission to show anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond to my learned friend. I wasn't now referring to the task given to the witness by the Prosecutor, but what follows from the witness's expert report and what some 15 or 20 minutes ago the witness said. He wished to show that everybody knew what the nature of the conflicts was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, can we come back to my question now. In your expert report, did you wish to show that everybody on the territory of the former Yugoslavia was aware of the nature of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would only refine that slightly to say that I don't think everybody in the former Yugoslavia would have known the nature of the conflict, but any literate, engaged adult would understand the nature of the conflict. I don't know if you were using the term" everybody" in its more specific meaning or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, what were the sources on the basis of which you could conclude whether someone understood the nature of the conflict or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a question that's rather wide open, but I could think of only one way to approach it. I couldn't go back and interview people at the time. Interviewing people today about what they knew in 1991 or 1992 would be a hopeless task, that's why memoirs are such unreliable sources. The only way I could approach the question really, in my view, is by looking at the press at the time. I simply don't know another way to do it. I don't -- I mean, the bottom line is I don't really know if we can absolutely conclude anything. I think that we can extrapolate from my report and from the conclusions in the report. I think it's reliable. I think it's the best that can be done to come to some type of -- slow down. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please, sorry. If I might go back to my question, if you based yourself primarily or exclusively on the press, you cannot tell us whether or how people understood the nature of the conflict. What you can tell us about is how the conflict was presented in the press; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. You told us that you based your expert report on the writings of the political weeklies, Danas and Vreme; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used also some Western, well, that is American press, and I looked, you know, I did look at other weeklies, but I didn't use them. And the reason I chose not to use them was that they tended to present an even more violent picture of what was happening in Yugoslavia. And there is, I would say, at this point evidence that much of the press, in its most extreme formulations, was inventive, that a lot of the press coverage, especially the most extreme coverage, was occasionally unreliable. So, yes, I relied on Danas and Vreme for the Yugoslav press for --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me for interrupting you, but I have little time at my disposal, which is why I would like your answers to be shorter. Can we agree on the following: The American press or any other foreign press would not be relevant if we wanted to know what was widely known, what was common knowledge in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that it would not be as critical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. You told us, yesterday, that you used the weeklies, Danas and Vreme, and that you also read Nin, and you mentioned the Hrvatski Tjednik. With respect to the Hrvatski Tjednik, as I come from Croatia and I think I know the Croatian media rather well, especially in the early 1990s, but quite honestly I have no idea what weekly that is. So could you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was actually hoping that I would have an occasion to do so. I don't actually, when I said that yesterday, I thought that I was right; but when I went home last night, or back to my hotel room, I realise I'm not actually sure of what the name of the Tudjman regime sponsored weekly was, and I readily admit that I could have the name wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I also don't know what weekly you mean, so I won't enumerate all the ones that existed at the time. Can we then conclude that you based your conclusions on Danas and Vreme, these two weeklies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you read those weeklies in 1990 to 1992 or later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where in the early 1990s you read these weeklies and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1991 and early 1992, I lived in the San Francisco Bay area and I made a weekly trip to a newsstand in Berkeley, where I bought them, and I still have many of them sitting in my box at work. Also, I can add that at some points, during that time, I was in Indiana, at Indiana University, which subscribed to both of them and more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the 1990s, what other newspapers or journals from Serbia and Croatia did you read, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read Nin. I read Interview from Serbia as long as it came out. I read -- I did not read many newspapers, at least not regularly. I read Duga, also from Belgrade. For a short time there was -- well, actually, I'm not sure if it was a short time or not, but for a short time, I read articles from something -- I believe it was called Hrvatski Vojnik, again, not necessarily a mainstream journal. I -- I'm sure there were others. I was able to get Glas Slavonije, oddly enough, at that Berkeley newsstand, so occasionally I bought it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you were preparing this expert report we are now discussing, did you rely on your reading back then, or did you re-read these weeklies we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I re-read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us based on what did you conclude that Vreme and Danas are representative weeklies, representative of public opinion in Croatia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I don't think that I would conclude that they were representative of public opinion in Croatia and Serbia. I would conclude, rather - and I think this is the general consensus, at least in the United States. Obviously, there is probably an inherent bias there - I would conclude that they were the most reliable. I purposely did not include journals, news magazines, that were considered to - I'm trying to find the proper word for this - that might have glorified the violence, let's say. I was not looking for the most extreme examples. It would have made my case probably more convincing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Without going into the correctness of your conclusion and whether I agree with it or not, Dr. Miller, I wish to clarify the following point. You might consider these weeklies to be the most reliable; but if it was your task to show what was generally known, then you should have relied on media which were representative, or rather, the media read by the greatest percentage of the population. Can you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can agree with you on that, I mean, in a sense. I can agree with you, and I have read that media. I guess it's ironic that I chose not to include that media because I thought that the picture that it drew was unreliable. It would have contributed to my own conclusion if I had included it, and so perhaps I should have. But the picture that we find in Danas and Vreme, insofar as, you know, the nature of the violence, the nature of the wars, is more moderate than the picture we would find in most of those other journals. That's a general conclusion based on, for the most part, reading I did during the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that Vreme has such a small circulation that, without the assistance of foreign donors, it would not have survived on the market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Danas, in the early 1990s, had such a small circulation that that was one of the main reasons why in the autumn of 1992 it stopped publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware that that's one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Miller, have you ever heard that, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, about 10 per cent of the population reads no newspapers at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpreter's correction: or any newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- that only 10 per cent of the population actually reads newspapers or gets information by electronic means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not have heard that, but I would believe it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. I would like to thank my friend who told me my question was not correctly recorded. I said that 10 per cent of the population reads newspapers; whereas, 90 per cent of the population receives information exclusively from the electronic media; although, I assume that you understood my question and that your answer remains the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, you understood my question. You speak Serbian, Croatian, Bosniak, whatever you wish to call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's why you're able to read this press in the original; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm certainly able to read this press in the original. In the preparation of this report, I had to access Vreme, for the most part, in English translation. Originally, of course, I did read it in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Miller, can we agree that, in the early 1990s, we cannot refer to the territory of the former Yugoslavia as a kind of unified market. It would be more proper to speak of the Serbian, Croatian, or Bosnian-Herzegovinian market; and when I refer to "market," I'm referring to it, of course, from the media aspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we then agree that something that might be widely known on the Serbian media market might be completely unknown on the Croatian media market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would agree intellectually, but my report actually doesn't discriminate between Serbs and Croats. The evidence is drawn from both, and the treatments of the war on both sides were essentially the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I was not trying to imply anything. I just wanted to use my question as a basis for the following: Dr. Miller, did you investigate how many inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina reads the weeklies, Vreme and Danas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we agree that based on the writings of the Belgrade weekly, Vreme, and the Zagreb weekly, Danas, we cannot speak of what was widely known on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, generally I suppose that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you just be very brief in your reply, please. Do we agree or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be very brief. I can be quite brief. Okay. I'm sorry. But I think we all know that Bosnia had all three populations. I mean, I spent time in Sarajevo, and I know that; whereas, Vreme might not have been read in Zagreb and Danas might not have been read in Belgrade. I actually think and I would -- I think that they were both read in Sarajevo by the respective populations. It was a divided market.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, when I'm asking you this, I don't have in mind just some dozen people who in Zagreb, Belgrade, and Sarajevo might have read weeklies from the territory of the whole of the former Yugoslavia. Maybe more than a dozen, but anyway. We're talking about something that is generally known and accepted now, that is, the broad population, the population at large. So, if you told me -- if you said to me that you don't know whether and to what extent Danas and Vreme were sold on the market of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then my logical next question would be: Would it be correct to conclude that Vreme and Danas cannot be a basis for drawing conclusions about something that was general knowledge on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I'm not talking about some dozen intellectuals in Sarajevo. I'm talking about the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina in general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel comfortable extrapolating from a broader reading.
