I told you already that I excluded the writings of other journals that were probably more widely read, I guess that was a mistake, which tell the same story, essentially. Obviously, I could find differences. But strictly speaking about those two journals, I suppose we cannot conclude that everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina read them. That would obviously be absurd.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, we're not discussing whether everybody read them. Of course not. Everybody did. That is not being challenged. What we're talking about is this: Do you have any proof and evidence that anyone read Vreme or Danas at that time, at the beginning of the 1990s in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no proof that anybody read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Dr. Miller, would you agree with me when I say that your expert report, based on the writings of the Belgrade weekly, Vreme, and the Zagreb weekly, Danas, cannot be a reliable indicator about what was generally known, for example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of the 1990s? Just briefly, please, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it can. I think it can because I read more widely, and this is a boiled-down version of wider reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, I'm not asking you whether you have any knowledge and whether you could tell us what was generally known in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I don't doubt that you do have such knowledge. What I'm asking you is exclusively with regard to your expert report, which is based as you, yourself, said on those two weeklies. So, based on those two weeklies, can the report be a reliable indicator of what was common knowledge in Bosnia-Herzegovina or generally known in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992? I'm sure you find it difficult to answer that question, but please try and be frank and honest in answering it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's as reliable as anything could be. I think determining what public opinion or what knowledge was in 1991 is very difficult. I think the conclusions in my report are drawn from a broader reading than just Danas and Vreme, and that it's probably the best we could do in determining what was common knowledge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Dr. Miller, in your first expert report or the first part of your report, did you want to tell us the characteristics and patterns of the conflict on the basis of your own opinion, and that you weren't that interested in what was generally known in -- on individual markets of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I understand the question. In the first part of the conflict -- first part of my report ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the first report, because we have two reports, so the first report, since you base yourself on the American press, the European press, sources you don't mention here, but you make certain conclusions. And on the basis of all that, one could conclude that you, in fact, provided your own vision of the nature of the conflict and that you were less interested or dealt less with what was generally known. And we interested in what was generally known in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't actually think my opinion is present here, and I did my best to show what I think was generally known.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, my last question from this set of questions. If you wanted to show us what was generally known on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, why did you not analyse a single publication printed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Sarajevo had a very rich publications activity compared to Belgrade -- which could be compared to the output in Belgrade and Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could have, but I wasn't actually asked to focus on what was generally known in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, I understand the nature of the case, but that's not what I was asked. I was asked what was generally known on the territory, in general, the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my final question: So you're saying that you didn't deal with what was generally known on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now have one more question for you, Dr. Miller, and it's this: Let's assume that the characteristics and patterns of the conflict, as being an ethnic conflict and everything that you state in your first report is correct, let's assume that. Now, do you consider that it would be logical to expect that the government, which decides to establish an army, establishes an army made up of the members of its own nation, own ethnic group; in other words, not to set up a multi-national, multi-ethnic, multi-confessional army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would expect that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, are you aware that, in Herceg-Bosna, the HVO or the government or the authorities, whatever you like to call these structures that were in charge of that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they formed an army that was called the HVO, which was composed of both Croats and Muslims and Serbs and members of other nations and nationalities, including those who declared themselves as undeclared; and that certain parts of Herceg-Bosna, especially around Mostar, there were more Muslims than there were Croats in some brigades? Did you ever hear of that? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware of that. I was aware that, early in the war, the ethnic composition of various armies was more complicated than it became later on. That doesn't surprise me to hear you explain that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were you also aware of the fact that this national ethnic composition within the HVO existed until mid-1993, and I'm not going to burden you with an event that took place on the 30th of June, 1993, which is well-known to Their Honours. Do you know and were you aware that this multi-national HVO remained that way until mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't have been able to say precisely until when it went -- lasted, but I'll accept your word.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, could we agree, you and I, that if the HVO was indeed established on a multi-ethnic basis, that the power and authority that created such an army, that established such an army, did not have the intention, nor did it expect, that it would ever go to war with the Muslims or the Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would that be a logical conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that calls for pure speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't consider that it is pure speculation. I consider that it is a logical conclusion on the basis of the premises made by Dr. Miller in his first expert report that we're discussing at present, because if the ethnic conflict was the basic characteristic and if, as the witness said, we could have expected violence against the members of an opposite ethnic group, then it would be logical to conclude this thing about the army. And I'd like to give the witness a chance to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to read the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat it for you, or you can read it, whichever you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll read it. It's fine. Thank you. Again, I have no idea. I could not read the minds of the leadership of the HVO. I don't think that question actually calls for a logical conclusion. It's too speculative for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If it is speculative, as you say, then thank you, Dr. Miller.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add a question that just follows the last question of Ms. Alaburic. Yesterday, we have discussed at some length about a statement you made that the HVO was not prepared to join a unitarian army of the BiH and it has been shown that there would, in fact, be two armies, so that was very natural. Now, is it correct that, according to the agreements, there ought to have been one joint army for the Federation? That an army of the Federation ought to have been forged of Croat and Bosniak soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean after the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume so. But if this is another yes or no question, I cannot say precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Have you found any evidence in your research that this actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That the armies unified and became one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, please go ahead -- just a moment. Mr. Petkovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just have one question to ask, perhaps it's technical, perhaps not, depending on how much the witness knows, if I might be able to pose it. Does the witness know that the army of the Federation was composed of two components and that that was provided for by law: One component was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the other component was the HVO, and that that's how the organized units existed. The HVO represented the first Croatian unity according to the law that was passed after all the agreements, that the army of the Federation had two components.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you, and that's what it says in the law: One component was the army and the other component was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With that sort of clarity, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the document shown you by the Prosecutor yesterday, did you see the relationship in the distribution of forces and resources, or rather, resources that they received from other countries, the United States and other western countries, that of the 287 tanks, the army was given 100-odd and the rest went to the HVO. So who was in charge of this distribution? The Americans were, General Warner and all the others. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm waiting for my microphone to come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm waiting on the microphone, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just object to Mr. Petkovic's reference to the document. The Prosecution wasn't allowed to use the document, and I don't think it's appropriate for the Defence to use the same document; although, I'd be happy to use it if everyone's in agreement on that. But it's either in for all sides or it's not in for any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The part of the document that was objected to was the one portion of it which was quite obvious to the Trial Chamber that there was no signature to, there was no date to it. There were other documents attached to it, but I think the question the way it was posed is a -- is quite appropriate, because it refers to a particular document, that obviously there were some figures to it. And I think it's quite appropriate. But in any event, the essence of the question itself is a question that should be put to this witness. Was he aware of that? Who was distributing? Because this is a follow-up, Judge Trechsel, on your question, and so I think it's very relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I don't see why the Prosecutor is objecting. What is he afraid of?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's be fair, Mr. Karnavas. I'm certainly not afraid of the evidence. I do believe in fair play. I believe, if one side is not allowed to use an exhibit, the other side shouldn't be able to use it either. I pointed out, at the time, that the document was a whole document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you say that you were not allowed to use the exhibit. Which exhibit are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the one that Mr. Praljak -- excuse me, Mr. Petkovic is just referring to. I think it was 10267, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think I can assist --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers switch on their microphones when speaking, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presiding Judge asked a question connected with the document and the number of tanks was mentioned and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to interfere here because I made the observation that this document had no signature, et cetera. That referred to the 18-page document. There were annexes to this document to which I have not referred. I must say I was even somewhat surprised that the Prosecution did not continue with these other documents, but it was not my task to do it or to insight that. So I think there is no unfairness if Mr. Petkovic is asking the question he is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There must have been a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There may have been, Your Honour, as I took pains to point out to the Chamber yesterday. The document was received in exactly the form -- it was in a sense one document at the time the Prosecution received it. It was combined. All these documents were combined. And since it was presented as one collective document, that's exactly the form it was found in the files of the archive, I understood Your Honours to say that none of the documents -- since it was one document, if it was a question about a part of the document, the entire document could not be used. That was my understanding. But I'll be happy to come back, perhaps, to other parts of it if given the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one other question, with your permission, please. The army of the Federation was not established pursuant to this document. This is a report. The army of the Federation has a law and regulations, according to which it was established, and that document is still in existence. It still exists in the archive of the Federation and in the army of the Federation. And I claim and I am saying that a document exists, brought in the level of the Federation, which says that the army of the Federation has two components: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council. That document does exist at Federation level. It can be found today in the Defence Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not speaking off the top of my head. This is just a report, which somebody wrote, but I'd like to refer you to that. The document is titled, "The basic premises of establishment or ratio of forces," something like that, but I'll do my best to find it. So the document does exist. It does exist. It refers to the establishment of the Bosnian-Herzegovinan army, and it did have two components. So there were two components of the army of the Federation, and Mr. Sotka was the commander of the Croatian component within the army of the Federation. So we have a document at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina which we can bring in. Now, this is a document that somebody used for some facts and figures and sent out to someone. Well, we can't see who compiled it, who signed it. It was an intelligence matter anyway, quite obviously. But there's a real document, stating that the army of the Federation has two components: The army and the HVO, and that's when there was a uniform, united BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've heard what Mr. Petkovic has just said. According to him, based not on this document but on another official text, the army of the Federation was made up of two components: The HVO and the ABiH. What do you think of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason to dispute it, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Dr. Miller, my name is Peter Murphy. I am one of the counsel representing Bruno Stojic. I would like to ask you about an answer you gave to my colleague, Ms. Alaburic, a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: For the record it's page 85, line 21 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You said that you were not looking for the most extreme examples and you said, and I'm going to quote: "It would have made my case probably more convincing." When you use the phrase "made my case more convincing," would you explain to the Trial Chamber what case you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my paper obviously, I hope. It's taken for granted that it has a thesis. The thesis is that the characteristics that I've described were widely known, and that's my case. I mean, that's what I mean when I say "my case." My thesis would have been easier to demonstrate. But part of my job is to evaluate the validity of evidence. And something that I think is commonly known about the Yugoslav and post-Yugoslav medias is that much of it systematically exaggerated events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, the reason for my question was simply that, at an earlier time in Ms. Alaburic's cross-examination, she asked a question, and Mr. Scott interrupted to emphasise that you were not asked to reach any particular conclusion, but to investigate certain matters. I suggest to you, based on your answer, that, in fact, your report was driven towards a predetermined conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I disagree completely. I'm asked to write a report. I have a conclusion. I write a report, it has a conclusion, it has a thesis. It could -- so I was not asked to produce any particular conclusion, and it was not a predisposition, at least not insofar as I did -- I mean,, obviously, I experienced the 1990s, and so I had a fair idea what to expect, but I disagree with that formulation completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to ask you about one further thing relating to Herceg-Bosna. This is really about your second report on the continuation of Herceg-Bosna. You're aware, of course, that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was set up or proclaimed in November of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that was before the international community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Within the same broad time-frame, the Bosnian Serbs also established certain structures, political structures, that, in due course, transmuted into Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now when the -- as a result of the Dayton Peace Accords, Republika Srpska then became a constituent of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that during the -- certainly during the war, the international community made much the same criticism of Republika Srpska that it did of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In other words, that it was an essentially illegal state which was -- had been implanted on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the basic criticism, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I suppose we could parse words, but sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But what's happened today through historical circumstances is that Republika Srpska has, in a sense, been legitimatised through the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, since Dayton, would you also agree that there has been considerable dissatisfaction with the political structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the part of all three constituent peoples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And, in fact, on more than occasion, the Office of the High Representative has had to make alterations to the constitution to try to keep everyone happy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would accept that, although I could not specify the alterations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, we don't need to be specific. Is it also within your knowledge that, even today, there is considerable political pressure among all three peoples to make fundamental changes to the Dayton structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And would you also not -- would you also agree with me that, in a democratic society, the Bosnian Croats, together with the other peoples, have a right to lobby politically for the changes they would like to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And so, when you refer in your report to, I think you used the word, intransigence on part of certain Bosnian Croats, would you also agree, to be fair, that that could also be seen as simply a resolute determination to try to get the changes that they want, to have those changes brought about, through the political process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that's a possible interpretation, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have re-examination? If you only need a quarter of an hour, we could finish today with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that I would be more than a quarter of an hour -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- in fact, I'm just now, in light of the discussion about the documents, I'm just now re-reading that one set of documents. So, in light of the fact that I'll need more than 15 minutes, I would ask to conduct the re-direct tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Am I to understand that he is now moving to re-open the direct examination; and if so, could we have concrete answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, because, again, I'm just looking back at these documents, which I had understood, perhaps, in error, had been excluded, and I would like an opportunity to review those otherwise conduct re-direct in an appropriate manner. This coming down to the last five or ten minutes and being rushed, which has happened to the Prosecution repeatedly, is not appropriate. We have the time, the witness is scheduled, and I would ask to conduct my re-direct tomorrow morning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have no objections to him asking for the time to prepare, if he's not prepared to continue right now. But if he does decide to re-open, and if the Trial Chamber does invite him to go ahead and re-open, obviously, we are entitled to cross-examination, at least to that portion, and I am sure Mr. Scott will agree with me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is quite clear in my mind, Mr. Scott, that tomorrow you will ask questions, additional questions, that are related to the questions that came up during the cross-examination. The re-examination is not supposed to -- it's not the same as the examination-in-chief. It is re-examination, additional questions. Witness, unfortunately, I thought perhaps you might be able to go home today, but you will have to come back tomorrow morning. The hearing will begin tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.; and in principle, it should be fairly brief. So I would invite all of you to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we adjourn, since we have a few minutes left, and so that I don't take any time, because I know Your Honour has a plenary meeting to go to tomorrow morning, I'm not sure how long it will last. Your Honour, tomorrow morning will be my last appearance in any court as an advocate after some 35 years. Obviously, that's a subject of very mixed emotions for me today. I would like to say what a privilege it's been to practice at this Tribunal, and, particularly, in front of this distinguished Trial Chamber, and in the company of such distinguished and abled colleagues. Your Honour, I would also like to extend my best wishes to the accused, and to say, in particular, what a privilege it has been that my last case should have been to represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. Your Honour, I thank you for your courtesy towards me and your attention through this long process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Murphy. On behalf of my colleagues and Judge Mindua, who is not here today, as he is in the Dragomir Milosevic case today, I've said this before, but, of course, we wish you all the best. All of our wishes for great success in your new career, career as a judge. That is an extremely difficult one as we experience on a daily basis. But I know that thanks to your extraordinary qualities that you have shown in your 35 years as a lawyer, you will have no difficulty in fulfilling this very noble mission as a judge. And, in the future, we will be very happy to meet with you again in other contexts. At any rate, please be assured of all our best wishes for this new part of your career. So the time has come and we meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
